1)	We will use a series of generalised linear mixed effects model in R to analyse our results. As in our first experiment (in prep), all models will include by-subject and by-item random intercepts. 
2)  By default we will estimate models using glmer as for our first experiment (in prep) but if there are problems with convergence, we will switch to Bayesian estimation using the brms package (version 2.5.0).
3)  To select the fixed effects in the model, we will compare progressively simpler with more complex models until the best goodness-of-fit is reached, indicating the most parsimonious model. Variables are selected in 3 blocks of predictors of interest (Concept-Level, Exemplar-Level, No-Interest). First, the full model will be fitted, then we will reduce model complexity by removing blocks of variables in the order: Concept-Level, Exemplar-Level, No-Interest variables, again following our first experiment (in prep). 
4)	In addition to the main effects of selected blocks of variables, we will test main effects and interactions of age x condition, and higher-order interactions of age and condition with the Concept-level and Exemplar level variables included in the selected model (see 3).    
5)	As the No-Interest variables are used only for controlling potential confounding effects, and are moderately correlated, we will perform a data reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with the prcomp function in R. Following a varimax rotation we will select sufficient components to account for at least 85% of the variance.
6)	Once the best model is chosen, we will run the follow-up analyses.


Follow-up analysis
We will conduct post hoc tests with correction for multiple comparisons using Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment using p.adjusted function in R. These will be implemented separately for two families of comparisons. These will be applied first in the young group alone, and across both age groups (for effects involving age only). Similar tests will be done in the older group only to shed light on interactions between age and experimental variables of interest:
1)	All main effects and interactions that include the Concept-Level variable (i.e., semantic confusability).
2)	All main effects and interactions that include the Item-Level variables (i.e., C1 and C2 HMax variables, colour similarity, image exemplarity).
paper_c1: As in Experiment 1, there was decisive evidence in favor of the full model including conceptlevel, item-level, and confounds principal component variables, relative to simpler models (see Supplemental Table 9). The full model was the most parsimonious, receiving the lowest AICc score (AICc = 17597.96), and substantial weight (AICc weight = 0.89) relative to the other models, with an evidence ratio between the top-ranked model and the second-ranked model of 7.83. This result was also supported by a significant LRT in favor of the full relative to the model ranked second on the basis of AIC (χ2(7) = 18.16, p = 0.011). Unlike Experiment 1, BIC now provided evidence in favor of the model with both concept- and-item level variables as the most parsimonious model (BIC = 17780.99). The results of the mixed effects analysis of the full model are shown below in Table 3, and illustrated in Figure 3. All the p-values are FDR-multiple comparison corrected (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Raw recognition responses by item type are reported in Supplemental Figure 6.

confusability metrics are given in the online supplemental material

identical to those used in Experiment 1, we used the same concept familiarity values collected previously. The main preregistered statistical analyses collapsed across the large and small study set sizes were

size (i.e., set size 8 vs set size 2), but as this variable had no significant effects we focus here on the results collapsed over the two set

phase RTs (results not reported; see OSF https://osf.io/ndk83/).

Screening: 
●	Anxiety: Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI; Beck et al., 1988)
○	Participants will be excluded if they report a cumulative score of 26 points or higher indicating clinically relevant levels of anxiety on the BAI.
●	Depression: Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9; Kroenke et al., 2001)
○	Participants will be excluded if they report a cumulative score of 14 points or higher indicating clinically relevant levels of depression on the PHQ-9. They will also be excluded from the study if they score higher than 0 on the item assessing suicidal tendencies. If current suicidal tendencies are reported, individuals will be provided with the telephone number and link to the chat service of the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline and the emergency telephone number of North America.
●	Alexithymia: Toronto Alexithymia Scale-26 (TAS-26; Taylor et al., 1985)
○	Participants will be excluded if they report a cumulative score of 54 points or higher indicating clinically relevant levels of alexithymia on the TAS-26.

T1 Questionnaires & Video Training:
●	Socio-demographic Questions: Gender, age, ethnicity, marital status, highest level of obtained education, state of residence, time zone, sexual orientation, current occupation, number of children, current living situation, current and past diagnoses of mental disorders
●	Trait Empathy Assessments: 
○	Perspective Taking Scale of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; Davis, 1980)  
○	Toronto Empathy Questionnaire (TEQ; Spreng et al., 2009)
●	EER Assessment:
○	Interpersonal Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (IERQ, Hofmann et al., 2016)
●	Video Training: A training video for participants can be found as a separate attachment on OSF.

EMA Protocol: The full EMA protocol can be viewed as a separate document on OSF. The most important assessments will be explained in more detail below. 
●	Perceived emotions: Participants will indicate on an 11-point scale (0 = not at all to 10 = very much) the extent to which they perceived 16 selected emotions in their interaction partner as assessed by the PANAS-X (Watson & Clark, 1999). Eight of these emotion items will correspond to perceived positive affect, while the remaining 8 emotion items will correspond to perceived negative affect.
●	Empathy: Four components of empathy will be assessed with five items using an 11-point scale (0 = not at all to 10 = very much). Following Gilchrist et al. (2019) and Ringwald and Wright (2021), we will assess mentalizing with two items: The extent to which participants understood (1) the feelings and (2) the thoughts of their interaction partners. Experience sharing will be reported as the extent to which participants shared the emotions of their interaction partners. We will also assess empathic concern (“To what extent did you experience concerned feelings for the other person?”) and personal distress (“To what extent did you feel distressed because of the other person’s emotions?”). With each item, participants will be reminded to think back to their experiences when the situation actually occurred. Higher scores on empathy scales will indicate higher empathy.
●	Regulation strategies: Participants will rate for 17 EER strategies the extent to which they employed them in their social interaction on an 11-point scale (0 = not at all to 10 = very much): Distraction, positive reappraisal, cognitive reappraisal, acceptance, soothing, validation, touch, rumination, avoidance, approach, problem solving, support, social modeling, perspective taking, humor, reassurance, and worry. 
●	Regulation goals: Participants will first report whether they wanted to influence the emotions of the other person (0 = not at all to 10 = very much). If participants answered not at all, their survey will be completed as they did not form a regulation goal. In case they score at least 1 point on the scale, they will be asked about the extent to which they wanted to increase, decrease, or maintain the emotions for positive and negative affect emotion items separately (0 = not at all to 10 = very much). Positive and negative emotion items for this question will only include emotions that were rated 1 or higher on the perceived emotions assessment.
paper_c1:
EMA Measures. We did not consider group interactions and
instructed participants to report on their most emotional dyadic interactions. This modification was due to a significant decrease in power
when differentiating between group and dyadic interactions. Only
measures different from Study 1 are presented.
State Empathy. We used an 11-point Likert scale (0 = not at all
to 10 = very much) to decrease participant burden as all other items
were rated on that scale. Mentalizing items were identical to Study 1.
To quantify experience sharing, participants reported how much
they shared the regulatees’ emotions. To ask participants about emotion transference (Study 1) implicated experience sharing as an automatic, reflexive process. However, experience sharing might be
more accurately characterized as an active and motivated process
(Zaki, 2014). Given that a core feature of IER is its goaldirectedness, we wanted to explore this active account of experience
sharing. To assess empathic concern, we adapted an item (“I have
tender, concerned feelings for people less fortunate than me”) of
the Toronto Empathy Questionnaire (TEQ; Spreng et al., 2009) for
EMA use by asking participants to indicate the extent to which
they experienced concerned feelings for the regulatees. As the
TEQ (Spreng et al., 2009) was created via the reduction of dimensions in preexisting empathy measures, the item used in our study
originates from the Empathic Concern subscale of the
Interpersonal Reactivity Index (Davis, 1983). To assess personal distress, we adapted the “distressed” item by Fabi et al. (2019), who
assessed momentary personal distress. Specifically, participants
rated how distressed they felt because of the regulatees’ emotions.
The within- and between-person reliabilities for empathy components were .50 and .93 and are acceptable (Nezlek, 2017).
Perceived State Emotions. We used the discrete emotion items
from the English version of the PANAS-X (D. Watson & Clark,
1994) equivalent to the German items in Study 1. In addition, we
also assessed the negative emotion item “distress.” The withinsubject reliability was .66 for positive emotions and .70 for negative
emotions. The between-subject reliabilities were .97 and .98, respectively, and are acceptable (Nezlek, 2017).
IER Goals. IER goals were assessed with multiple items on the
11-point Likert scale (0 = not at all to 10 = very much). Initially, participants answered the question, “Did you want to influence the
other person’s emotions?” If participants selected zero, they were
classified as not having had a regulation goal, and the respective
EMA survey ended. If participants indicated anything other than
zero, they subsequently rated their specific IER goals for positive
and negative emotions on three items, respectively. All three items
listed either positive or negative emotions participants indicated
with anything other than zero on the perceived state emotions assessment. In other words, if a participant selected four negative and four
positive emotions on the perceived state emotions assessment, the
following questions listed only the indicated eight emotions. For
negative and positive emotions separately, participants then rated
the extent to which they wanted to decrease, maintain, or increase
the other’s emotions. For instance, participants rated the item “I
wanted to decrease the other person’s [selected positive emotions]”
and “I wanted to decrease the other person’s [selected negative
emotions].” [...]
They were further screened for clinical levels of
depression, anxiety, alexithymia, and suicidal ideation, all of which
have been found to impair IER processes (Erickson & Newman,
2007; Hofmann, 2014; Spitzer et al., 2005; Vanderlind et al., 2020).

Analyses for EER strategy selection
-	To investigate links between empathic components and strategy selection, we will use the statsBy function in the R package ‘psych’, which decomposes the observed correlations between empathy and strategy use into the within-person and between-person associations. prereg_c2:
To investigate whether people tend to interpret rare words as more similar in meaning to similar-sounding words than distributional semantic models predict, we will conduct a semantic relatedness decision experiment. Participants will decide whether a cue word (e.g., "dodge") is related to a target word. The target word is either non-arbitrary (overlapping with an attractor word in both form and meaning, e.g., "evade," which overlaps with "avoid") or is an arbitrary control (e.g., "elude," which is similar in meaning to "evade"). We designed the non-arbitrary targets and the arbitrary controls to be equally similar in meaning to the cues, as measured by distributional information (LSA, CBOW, and HAL cosines).

Hypothesis 1: If rare words are interpreted as more similar in meaning to similar-sounding words than distributional information would suggest, then participants will make more "yes" decisions about non-arbitrary targets than about arbitrary controls. That is, participants will be more likely to decide that "evade" is semantically related to "dodge" than that "elude" is.

Hypothesis 2: If rare words are interpreted as more similar in meaning to similar-sounding words than distributional information would suggest, then participants will make faster "yes" decisions about non-arbitrary targets than about arbitrary controls.
paper_c2:
This leads to our first research question: Do similar-sounding words affect how we
interpret “real” words—known words learned in rich environments? Apparent examples of form-
based semantic shifts, like sheen towards shine or override towards overwrite, could be coincidental, so we are interested in cases where form leads people to make inferences that
outpace diachronic changes in distribution. We are also interested in whether such cases, if any,
confer an advantage in word meaning access. Are form-based semantic shifts a cautionary tale
about the risks of non-arbitrariness, where distinctions cease to make a difference? Or do similar-
sounding words serve as a scaffolding that helps people access otherwise fuzzy meanings?
[...]
We predict that people will decide that non-arbitrary targets are
semantically related to cues more often than arbitrary targets are (such as elude). We also predict
that they will make those decisions faster for non-arbitrary targets.

Stimuli were presented on a 1280 3 1024 resolution Dell 2200
monitor in a darkened room. The experiment was coded and pre-
sented using MATLAB (Mathworks Inc.) and PsychToolbox (Brai-
nard, 1997). Responses were recorded with a calibrated RT box (Li
et al., 2010) on an Ubuntu 14.04 operating system.
Stimuli were composite faces consisting of a top half extending
from the forehead to the upper part of the nose and a bottom half
extending from the lower part of the nose to the neckline (see Figure
4). To create the halves, a set of 54 base faces were selected from
Kayser (1997; see also Steyvers, 1999). Twenty morph sets were
then created by selecting four base faces (A, B, C, and D) at random,
with replacement across sets, and morphing them together using a eld morphing technique (see Steyvers, 1999) such that each morph
set was a 3 3 3 matrix with variation between A and B forming one
dimension and between C and D forming the other dimension (see
Figure 3). Only the faces on the diagonals were used. On each trial, a
top face half and a bottom face half were randomly drawn from the
corner items of two morph sets to create a study composite face.
Hence, from the 20 morph sets, there were 80 possible top face
halves and 80 possible bottom face halves, yielding 6400 unique
faces.
The presentation of a study face was always followed by a test
face. Each half of the test face was drawn from the same morph set
as the respective half of the study face. A test face half could be the
same as the study face (S), differ by a low-discriminability change
(L), or differ by a high discriminability change (H). In terms of the
morph set in Figure 3, an L change is one step on both dimensions
of the morph space (e.g., the top-left vs the center), and an H
change is two steps on both dimensions (e.g., the top-left vs the bot-
tom-right).
The only difference between the aligned and misaligned stimuli
was that for the latter the face halves were horizontally offset by 85
pixels such that the edge of the bottom half lined up with the nose
of the top half (see the bottom row of Figure 4).
Participants sat at a viewing distance of 60 cm. Each aligned com-
posite was 400 3 340 pixels, subtending a visual angle of 6.688
3
5.678. Each misaligned composite was 400 3 425 pixels, subtend-
ing a visual angle of 6.688
3 7.098. A gap of 10 pixels provided a
smoother transition between the morphed halves and subtended a
visual angle of .178. A Gaussian blur was also applied to the edges
of each face.

vs H/L, and S/S vs H/H, with d’ expected to increase across those conditions if there is

Hypotheses: 
Our primary goal is to investigate how people perceive the contribution to society of unpaid assistance of close others in comparison to volunteering. We expect that compared to volunteering, unpaid assistance to close others (both hands-on assistance and information-based or remote care) will be perceived as:
- Less of a contribution to society and
- Reflecting less choice to help, 
In general (e.g., “In general, how much do hours spent providing hands-on unpaid assistance to close others contribute to society?” and “In general, how much do hours spent providing information-based or remote care (i.e., not hands-on) unpaid assistance to close others contribute to society?” vs. “In general, how much do hours spent doing formal volunteer work contribute to society?”) and 
Among people who engage in these helping behaviors (e.g., “How much do the hours you spend providing hands-on unpaid assistance to close others contribute to society?” and “How much do the hours you spend providing information-based or remote care (i.e., not hands-on) unpaid assistance to close others contribute to society?” vs. “How much do the hours you spend doing formal volunteer work contribute to society?”). 


Exploratory: 
- Mediating role of choice and obligation in perceived contribution: We will explore whether the perceived choice or obligation to help mediates the effect of the type of help (unpaid assistance to close others vs. volunteering) on perceived contribution to society in general and among people who engage in these helping behaviors. 
- Social class differences in helping behaviors: We will explore social class differences in unpaid assistance to close others and volunteering. 
-- We expect people in higher social class contexts to report higher rates of volunteering than people in lower social class contexts. 
-- We expect people in lower social class contexts to report higher rates of unpaid assistance to close others than people in higher social class contexts or to observe no significant difference between rates of unpaid assistance to close others by social class context. 
-- We will explore any potential differences between hands-on vs. information-based or remote care unpaid assistance. 
- Social class disparities in self-perceived social contribution and in relation to helping behaviors: We will explore social class differences in self-perceived social contribution and how self-perceived social contribution is related to engaging in unpaid assistance to close others and volunteering, perceptions of the contribution of these helping behaviors and the perceived choice or obligation to help for each of these helping behaviors. 
-- We expect people in lower social class contexts to report lower self-perceived social contribution than people in higher social class contexts. 
-- We expect volunteering (e.g., engaging in volunteering, perceptions of the contribution to society of volunteering, and perception of the amount of choice or obligation to volunteer) to be more strongly related to self-perceived social contribution than unpaid assistance to close others (e.g., engaging in unpaid assistance to close others, perceptions of the contribution to society of unpaid assistance to close others, and perception of the amount of choice or obligation to engage in unpaid assistance to close others). 
-- We will also explore how volunteering (e.g., engaging in volunteering, perceptions of the contribution to society of volunteering, and perception of the amount of choice or obligation to volunteer) versus unpaid assistance to close others (e.g., engaging in unpaid assistance to close others, perceptions of the contribution to society of unpaid assistance to close others, and perception of the amount of choice or obligation to engage in unpaid assistance to close others) relates to the social class disparity in self-perceived social contribution. 
-- We may explore if certain variables moderate the effect of other variables on self-perceived social contribution (e.g., perception of volunteering moderating the effect of hours spent volunteering). 
-- We may also explore how measures related to volunteering and unpaid assistance to close others predict the perception of the contribution of those helping behaviors (e.g., hours spent volunteering predicting the perceived value of those hours spent volunteering) and if any measures of volunteering and unpaid assistance to close others moderate the effect of other measures on the perceived contribution of volunteering or unpaid assistance to close others. 
- Association between self-perceived social contribution and measures of well-being, respect, and societal integration: We will explore how participants’ self-perceived social contribution relates to measures of their well-being, sense of respect, and societal integration, expecting self-perceived social contribution to be positively related to greater well-being, a greater sense of respect, and more societal integration. 
-- We may also explore social class disparities in measures of well-being, respect, and societal integration and whether self-perceived social contribution mediates any social class disparities in these outcomes. 
- Disparities in the perceived contribution of social groups: We will explore how people rate the contribution of income- and education-based social groups (e.g., “those making $26,000 or less per year”, “those with a high school degree or less education”). 
-- We will explore ratings reflecting participants’ own opinions as well as their ratings of what they think other people think (i.e., meta-perceptions). 
-- We expect that the distribution of contribution to society (e.g., 100% divided between five income or three education groups) will not be evenly distributed. For the five income groups, perceived contribution would be evenly distributed if each group is rated as contributing 20% to society. For the three education groups, perceived contribution would be evenly distributed if each group is rated as contributing 33% to society. 
-- We will explore if participants’ political party and/or ideology are associated with these ratings. 
- Associations between perceived contribution of social groups and support for redistribution and political participation among lower-income Americans: We will explore how the perceived contribution of income- and education-based social groups relate to support for redistribution and political participation among lower-income Americans. Specifically, we will investigate how the ratings of the lowest and highest income- and education-groups predict redistribution and political engagement. 
-- We expect that ratings of perceived contribution to society for the lowest income- and education-groups will be positively related to support for redistribution and political participation among lower-income Americans (i.e., higher ratings of contribution to society for the lowest income- and education-groups will be related to increased support for redistribution and political participation among lower-income Americans). 
-- We expect that ratings of perceived contribution to society for the highest income- and education-groups will be negatively related to support for redistribution and political participation among lower-income Americans (i.e., higher ratings of contribution to society for the highest income- and education-groups will be related to reduced support for redistribution and political participation among lower-income Americans). 
-- We may include participants’ political party and/or ideology are associated with the outcomes or moderate any effect of perceived contribution on the outcomes.

Social classes are cultural contexts that
vary in objective markers of status, such as educational attainment,
wealth and income, occupational status, and material resources as
well as in values, ways of living in the world, and patterns of self-
construal (Carey & Markus, 2017; Cohen & Varnum, 2016; Fiske,
2011; Kraus et al., 2011, 2019; Lamont, 2000; Markus & Conner,
2013; Snibbe & Markus, 2005; Stephens et al., 2012; Williams,
2017). Here, we index social class context using educational
attainment, as it is one of the most commonly used measures of
social class and is a strong predictor of a variety of outcomes (Case
& Deaton, 2015; Davis, 1982; Fiske & Markus, 2012; Stephens
et al., 2012; Williams, 2017).7 Participants with a high-school
degree or less education were coded as navigating lower social
class contexts and participants with a 4-year college degree or
more as navigating higher social class contexts. Across all studies,
participants in lower social class contexts reported lower incomes
and a greater likelihood of working lower status jobs (e.g., manual
or blue collar) compared to participants in higher social class
contexts, who had a greater likelihood of working higher status
jobs (e.g., professional or managerial; see Supplemental Material
for details). This pattern suggests that using dichotomized
education serves as a reasonable proxy for the broader construct
of social class.
[...]
Contribution to Society. Participants rated,“In general, how
much do hours spent [e.g., providing hands-on unpaid assistance to
close others, doing formal volunteer work] contribute to society?”
Ratings were on a scale from 1= no contribution at all to 5= an
enormous contribution (M = 2.81, SD= 1.33). 
[...]
Covariates. We included social class context (i.e., dichoto-
mized into those with or without a 4-year college degree), age,
gender, race (dichotomized as in Study 1), marital status (dichoto-
mized into currently married vs. not currently married), and working
status (dichotomized into currently working vs. not working) as
covariates in the analyses. We did not list working status as a
covariate in our preregistration; however, we added it to account for
any effects of employment on helping behaviors and perceptions of
those behaviors. Covariate descriptive statistics are reported in the
Supplemental Material.

To reduce participant burden, we utilized two versions of a daily
survey (Short and Full Version), one of which was sent to the participants via e-mail each day of the assessment period following

As part of an exploratory analysis, we will also examine the impact of age on the complete sum of all worry questions as well as each of the worry questions separately to determine if COVID19 has had any age-related effects in other domains.

We will also investigate the utility of using questions of virtual socializing and encountering others “face-to-face” as measures of social connectedness, although we believe both questions have significant limitations. These variables will be log transformed before being used in regression models. This reflects the expectation that these variables are more likely to have a logarithmic than linear relationship to mood outcomes—i.e., there will be a benefit of socializing and contact with people, but there will be diminishing returns to the benefit of these variables as the amount increase. In addition, the log transformation also reduces the significant positive skew and outliers in these variables. As such, our primary analyses are limited to their self-reported experience of social isolation/connectedness.

We will also investigate the utility of using step count as a measure of exercise, although this is limited to participants that owned a step counter during the assessment period and reported it (~40% of our data). To reduce the impact of a few large outliers in the step variable, we plan to exclude any observations more than three median absolute deviations from the median. This is a common outlier detection rule (Leys, Delacre, Mora, Lakens, & Ley, 2019).

responses (same hand vs. different hands) affected the size of spatial
S–R correspondence effects, whereas spatial distance did not. In particular, Wühr and Heuer (2018) observed larger Simon effects for a

paper_c2: In Experiment 1, we evaluated the effects of an unstructured background with little visual or semantic structure on search efficiency. A sandy beach scene with water elements was used as the background, and participants searched for a green turtle among black turtles (low similarity distractors, Experiment 1A) or among yellowish–green turtles (high similarity distractors, Experiment 1B). Search efficiency for the same target and distractors was also evaluated with two other backgrounds. A solid background was created by averaging the RGB values of the naturalistic background scene. This background condition provided us with a baseline for searching for the same items when no scene information is present, which is also the most often encountered condition in laboratory studies of search. Finally, a phase-scrambled background was created from the naturalistic beach background (e.g., Caddigan et al., 2017). This background maintained similar first-order image statistics as the beach background but scrambled the recognition of the elements in the scene (sand, wave, water), which allowed us to evaluate the effect of low-level features on search efficiency. Based on previous findings on efficient search, we expected to observe a logarithmic relationship between RTs and set size (Buetti et al., 2016; Lleras et al., 2020; Madison et al., 2018; Ng et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018). We also expected the logarithmic slopes to be sensitive to the similarity relationship between the target and distractors. Specifically, the slopes should be steeper in the high similarity than in the low similarity search condition. Regarding the effect of background on search performance, there are several possible ways in which background could impact search performance. With respect to search-related processes, it is possible that backgrounds will have no meaningful effects on search efficiency (see Wolfe et al., 2011). As mentioned earlier, it is also possible that complex backgrounds might slow down search efficiency, similar to how crowding and stimulus size have been shown to impact search efficiency (Madison et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018). This would result in inflated logarithmic slopes in the more complex background conditions compared to the solid background conditions. If recognition of the elements that make up the background image drives this effect, the increase in the logarithmic slopes should only be observed in the beach but not in the phase-scrambled background because, by design, the phase-scrambled image has no recognizable visual elements. If it is the presence of more complex visual features that drives the effect, then the increase in slopes should be observed with both backgrounds. It is also possible that background impacts nonsearch-related processes, such as the overall time required to identify the target in the absence of any distractors. These types of effects will be observed at the level of the intercepts of the logarithmic functions fitted to each participant’s performance. 1. The CSE will remain modality-specific as in our prior studies for either or both of two reasons. First, participants can easily categorize each trial as "visual" or "auditory" (Hazeltine et al., 2011). Second, participants will respond only to the probe in each trial, which reduces CSE magnitude, rather than to both the prime and probe, which increases CSE magnitude (Grant & Weissman, 2019). Critically, this hypothesis predicts a 3-way interaction among modality condition (repeat, switch), previous trial congruency (congruent, incongruent), and current trial congruency (congruent, incongruent).

2. The CSE will not remain modality-specific for one of two reasons. First, participants may have time to silently read the distractor word on the screen before the target word appears. If so, they may be able to use a common verbal code in both visual and auditory trials, thereby allowing participants to use a single modality-general task set to process both visual and auditory trials. Second, participants may have time to switch from one task set (e.g., visual) to another (e.g., auditory) before the target appears. If so, they be better able to modulate the response cued by the distractor to engender a CSE before the target appears. This hypothesis assumes that one must switch to the current-trial task set before one can "apply" one's memory of previous-trial congruency to modulate the response cued by the distractor in the current trial. These hypotheses predict an interaction between previous trial congruency and current trial congruency (i.e., a CSE) but not necessarily a 3-way interaction among modality condition, previous trial congruency, and current trial congruency.

In contrast, the binary coding view predicts that changing the
modality-specific task set will eliminate the CSE in a standard

the prime in the current trial does not constitute a repetition of the
previous trial’s overall S-R mapping (i.e., a repetition of both the
previous prime’s S-R mapping and the previous probe’s S-R mapping) that can independently trigger the retrieval of the previous
trial’s congruency. Indeed, neither the previous trial nor the current trial has an overall S-R mapping because participants use a
different S-R mapping for the prime (i.e., do not respond to the
stimulus) than for the probe (i.e., identify the stimulus by making
one of four possible keypresses). Thus, when the modality-specific
task set switches, neither the current task set nor the current S-R
mapping can trigger the retrieval of the previous trial’s congruency. For this reason, changing the modality-specific task
set should eliminate the CSE. Consistent with this prediction, the
CSE is smaller in the standard version of the unimodal (i.e., visual-modality) prime-probe task, wherein the overall S-R mapping
does not repeat, than in the modified version of the same task,

Measured variables
Independent Variable:

Perceived Responses to Capitalization Attempts
We measured participants’ perceptions of how their close others typically respond to when the participant shares a positive event using the Perceived Responses to Capitalization Attempts (PRCA; Gable et al., 2004). This 12-item measure is separated into four subscales: active-constructive, passive-constructive, active-destructive, and passive-destructive. Scores for each PRCA subscale will be calculated by averaging the three items of each subscale. A total composite score for perceived responses to capitalization will be calculated by subtracting the scores of the passive-constructive, active-destructive, and passive-destructive subscales from the active-constructive score. 

Instructions: Please take a moment to consider how your family, friends, and romantic partner (if you have one) respond when you tell them about something good that has happened to you.  For example, imagine that you come home and tell your friend about receiving a promotion at work, having a great conversation with someone, finishing a project, meeting someone interesting, winning a prize, or doing well on an exam or project at work or school. Please consider to what extent your family, friends, and partner do the following things in response to your good fortune.

7-point Scale: 1 (not at all true) to 7 (very true)

(1)	Active-constructive (averaged, 3 items)
a.	“They usually react to my good fortune enthusiastically.”
b.	“I sometimes get the sense that they are even more happy and excited than I am.”
c.	“They often ask a lot of questions and show genuine concern about the event.
(2)	Passive-constructive (averaged, 3 items)
a.	“They are silently supportive of the good things that occur to me.”
b.	“They try not to make a big deal out of it, but are happy for me.”
c.	“They say little, but I know he/she is happy for me.”
(3)	Active-destructive (averaged, 3 items)
a.	“They point out the potential problems or down sides of the good event.”
b.	“They often find a problem with it.”
c.	“They remind me that most good things have their bad aspects as well.”
(4)	Passive-destructive (averaged, 3 items)
a.	“They don’t pay much attention to me.”
b.	“Sometimes I get the impression that they don’t care much.
c.	“They often seem disinterested.”




Dependent Variables:

1. Momentary Gratitude (ecological momentary assessment measure)
Participants reported how much gratitude they were experiencing in the moment they received the survey notification.

Instructions: Please answer the following questions about your emotions at the time of the prompt. 

Scale: 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely)

I felt grateful.

2. Capitalization Attempts (ecological momentary assessment measure)
Participants reported whether they were engaged in capitalization efforts when they received each survey notification. 

Did you use any of the following strategies to influence your emotions at the time of the prompt?
•	I talked with another person about positive events

Scale: Yes or No

1. Age (in years)

2. Momentary Social Closeness (ecological momentary assessment measure)
Participants reported their degree of closeness with their interaction partner(s) for the most recent time they interacted with someone. 

Scale:
1 = Not at all
2 = Slightly
3 = Somewhat
4 = Moderately
5 = Extremely

How close do you feel to the person/people you were interacting with?

3. Most Recent Social Interaction (ecological momentary assessment measure)
Participants reported the most recent time they interacted with someone.

Scale:
1 = At the time of the prompt
2 = 1-30 minutes before the prompt
3 = 30-60 minutes before the prompt
4 = 1-2 hours before the prompt
5 = 2-3 hours before the prompt

When was the last time you interacted with someone?
paper_c2:
Measures

Active–Constructive PRCA
The PRCA scale (Gable et al., 2004) assesses a capitalizer’s perception of their close social partners’ responses when they share positive events in their life. This 12-item scale is divided into four
subscales of response types, each subscale consisting of three
items. Active–constructive (α = .66) was the subscale of particular
interest in the present study. When asked to “Please consider to
what extent your family, friends, and partner do the following things
in response to your good fortune,” participants responded to the
items using a scale that ranges from 1 (not at all true) to 7 (very true). Items for active–constructive include “They usually react to
my good fortune enthusiastically,”“I sometimes get the sense that
they are even more happy and excited than I am,” and “They often
ask a lot of questions and show genuine concern about the event.”
Active–constructive PRCA was calculated by averaging the score
of these three items.

Momentary Gratitude
Momentary gratitude was measured during the EMA component
of the study. At each survey prompt, participants were asked to report
how much gratitude they were experiencing in the moment they
received the survey notification. Responding to “I felt grateful,” participants rated how grateful they felt on a 7-point scale from 1 (not at
all) to 7 (extremely).

Momentary Social Closeness
Social closeness was reported during the EMA surveys to assess
the participants’ degree of closeness with their most recent social
interaction partner(s). Participants responded to the question “How
close do you feel to the person/people you were interacting with?”
on a 5-point scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely).

Momentary Capitalization
Capitalization attempts were captured during the EMA component
of the study through a prompt asking, “Did you use any of the following strategies to influence your emotions at the time of the prompt?”
Selecting (yes/no) “I talked with another person about positive events”
was used to indicate that the participant had engaged in a capitalization attempt. Participants were instructed that capitalization is when
you share or discuss positive things with others, such as sharing the
news that you got a promotion. To ensure comprehension, participants
were asked to provide an example of capitalization and an experimenter confirmed their understanding that capitalization involves
sharing an event, achievement, or good news with someone else.

Interaction Recency
The timing of participants’ most recent social interaction with
someone was measured by an EMA item asking, “When was the
last time you interacted with someone?” Participants reported their
interaction recency as: At the time of the prompt, 1–30 min before
the prompt, 30–60 min before the prompt, 1–2 hr before the prompt,
2–3 hr before the prompt, or more than 3 hr before the prompt.

Physical Health
The physical component score (α = .93) from the SF-36 Health
Survey Version 2 (Ware et al., 2000) was used to measure physical
health. Higher scores on the physical component indicates better
health

Analytic Plan
For the EMA variables, we calculated the person-mean for each individual by averaging their ratings across all prompts. Bivariate correlations were examined among active-constructive PRCA, age, frequency of momentary capitalization attempts (across all prompts), average momentary gratitude, average momentary closeness, physical health, and interaction recency. Correlations of the within-person variables were also assessed (see Table 2). 
Multilevel Modeling
We performed multilevel modeling (MLM) with prompts nested within person, included random slopes in all analyses and decomposed significant interactions using simple slopes (Aiken & West, 1991). We person-mean centered the within-person predictor variables and grand-mean centered the between-person predictor variables. Age was grand-mean centered. To examine effect sizes, we calculated semi-partial R2 (Edwards et al., 2008).
The first set of MLMs assessed how capitalization attempts (separated into within- and between-person components) predict momentary gratitude, testing age and social closeness (separated into within- and between-person components) as moderators of these effects. The second and third set of MLMs assessed how trait-level active-constructive PRCA predicts momentary gratitude and capitalization. Logistic MLMs were used when predicting momentary capitalization (a binary variable), including the models testing for age and both within- and between-person social closeness moderating the effects of active-constructive PRCA.
We conducted two types of robustness checks. First, we conducted an additional set of models controlling for social interaction recency. Social interaction recency was effect-coded such that having no social interaction within 30 min of the prompt was coded as –1 and having a social interaction within 30 min of the prompt was coded as +1. Then, this variable was personmean centered to calculate the within-person component and grand-mean centered to calculate the between-person component. Second, physical health was added as a covariate in all models including age because a large body of research suggests negatively valenced affectivity is associated with poor physical health (e.g., Pressman & Cohen, 2005; Chida & Hamer, 2008). Results for all models were unchanged when controlling for the covariates interaction recency and physical health (see Tables S1–S4 in Supplementary Materials).

The rate of temporal compression of videos during memory replay was estimated as the ratio of the actual video duration to the duration of its mental replay. [...]
On average, participants reported 33.57 actions per video in the complete condition, 95% CI [29.21, 37.12], and 25.87 actions per video in the ellipsis condition, 95% CI [22.92, 28.65]. A Yuen’s t-test showed that participants recalled more actions for complete than ellipsis videos, t = 3.14, p < .001, ξ = .47. To assess the density of recalled actions from the videos, we computed the number of reported actions per unit of time (i.e., per minute) of each video. The mean density of recalled actions in the two experimental conditions are shown on Figure 2B. Consistent with our prediction, a Yuen’s t-test revealed that the density of recalled actions was higher for ellipsis videos than for complete videos, t = -3.28, p = .003, ξ = .51.
We also estimated the time taken by participants to remember each action by dividing the duration of mental replay by the number of recalled actions. On average, participants took 2.85 seconds to remember an action in the complete condition, 95% CI [2.57, 3.19], and 2.77 seconds in the ellipse condition, 95% CI [2.48, 3.06]. A Yuen’s t-test showed that this difference was not statistically significant, t = 0.39, p = .711, ξ = .06.
Although not part of our preregistered analyses, we also examined to what extent the actions recalled in the complete condition corresponded to parts of the videos that were retained or deleted in the ellipsis condition.

Sample size rationale

We based our sample size on the analysis of a pilot study with 20 subjects. For each of those subjects, and separately for trials with hidden prior information, disclosed negative (fee) information, and disclosed positive (premium) information, we calculated the average ScanMatch similarity between the scanpaths of the given subject during the given type of trials and those of all other subjects during the same type of trials (data available on the OSF project page). We then conducted two paired two-tailed Wilcoxon tests: (1) of the difference between the average similarity between trials with hidden vs. disclosed negative information; and (2) of the difference between the average similarity between trials with hidden vs. disclosed positive information. Using GPower 3.1.9, for effect (1), we obtained an effect size of d = 0.359; and for effect (2) an effect size of 0.80. Based on the weaker of the two effects (1), two-tailed alpha = .05, and power = 0.90, we obtained a required sample size of 88. Accordingly, we will aim to recruit a number of subjects slightly above this value, i.e. approximately 100 subjects, so that the final sample after potential no-shows or exclusions would not fall below this threshold.

- in the example shown, those who drew the square would receive a positive (+15)

The experiments were conducted at a large private university and were approved
by the local research ethics committee.
Each participant was seated at a laptop with a 15.4-inch screen with resolution set

asking 50 survey participants to classify the translated words as positive or negative.

In the first part of the analysis, we will calculate pairwise ScanMatch similarities between all scanpaths (constructed by matching fixations to 35 AOIs, i.e. the fixed locations of words displayed on the screen). Next, we will compute the average similarity between every scanpath and those of other subjects registered in the same experimental condition (hidden information / fee / premium). We will use this as the outcome variable in a linear mixed model with random subject effects, the experimental condition as the main independent variable, and scanpath length and trial number as controls, to test if scanpath similarity is increased when the information is hidden. We will aim to replicate the results by using two alternative dependent variables: (1) a one-dimensional t-SNE transformation of the scanpath similarity matrix (based on the MATLAB t-SNEp implementation); (2) the 'rarer-probability' measure (obtained using the RarerProbability function embedded in Wolfram Mathematica 12.0) describing the extent to which a given 2-dimensional t-SNE representation of the scanpath is typical  among all scanpaths registered in the study (we expect to obtain larger values when prior information is hidden than when it is not).

In the second part of the analysis, we will randomly split all scanpaths into two groups (the training sample and the testing sample), and then repeatedly draw scanpath subsets ('training examples') of a given size (20, 40, or 60), registered during a given experimental condition, from the training sample. For each training example, we will calculate the average ScanMatch similarity between all scanpaths in the subset, as well as the average values of the rarer-probability and one-dimensional t-SNE variables described above. Using the drawn training examples, we will train a machine-learning algorithm (Gradient Boosted Trees and a benchmark standard Logistic Regression) predicting the experimental condition from the three input variables. We will then evaluate the trained algorithm on the testing sample, and then reverse the process (training on what used to be the testing sample and evaluating on the training sample). We will repeat this two-fold cross validation process 5 times, and evaluate if predictions are significantly above chance (and above those given by a benchmark model trained on average reaction times) using the 5-2 cross validation test and a permutation test. We will conduct this testing procedure for two cases: 1) distinguishing between the hidden condition and the fee condition; and 2) distinguishing between the hidden condition and the premium condition. 

The associated data analysis code (in the Wolfram Mathematica language) that we will use to carry out the procedures described in this section, taking a given raw eye-data set as input, is attached.

In accordance with our hypothesis, we examined a number of
measures of the participants’ cognitive processing of opinions. For
each measure as the dependent variable, we estimated a linear

mixed-effects model, each trial constituting a single observa-
tion. We included random subject intercept and slope effects to

allow for different observations of the same person being cor-
related, and to model the between-subjects variation of esti-
mated effects. The set of independent variables included two

binary experimental condition indicators (but no interaction
between them): “adjustment-disclosed” (1  either positive or

negative prior disclosure, 0 otherwise) and “adjustment-
disclosed-negative” (1  negative prior disclosure, 0 other-
wise). In this way, no disclosure constituted the baseline cate-
gory, the “adjustment-disclosed” coefficient measured the

difference between no disclosure and a positive one, and fi-
nally, “adjustment-disclosed-negative” measured the difference

between a negative and a positive disclosure.2 We also included
the trial number, the proportion of positive words in the opinion
grid, and the return gained in the previous trial as controls. All
variables were rescaled to [0, 1] and the full model estimation
results are presented in Table 1. [...]
As per
our preregistration, we used the following four predictors: (a) the
average similarity between the scanpaths making up the set; (b)
their average rarer-probability; (c) their average one-dimensional
scanpath representation score (used instead of its two-dimensional
variant due to the need to average the scores, see the Appendix);
and (d) the average number of words seen. As a benchmark, we
also evaluated a classifier based on the only noneye tracking
measure—the average viewing time across the group. To train both
classifiers, we used the LightGBM implementation of the Gradient
Boosted Decision Tree technique (Ke et al., 2017).

To evaluate the classifiers, we used 5–2 stratified cross-
validation. That is, we repeatedly (five times) randomly split the

whole individual-trial data into two folds, each containing an equal
share of each type of disclosure. For each split, we recorded the
accuracy of each of the two classifiers when trained on each of the
two folds and tested on the other. Prior to training and testing, we
randomly sampled from each fold groups consisting of a fixed

number of scanpaths belonging to different participants but asso-
ciated with the same, given disclosure type. We drew 10,000 of

such groups from each fold, with an equal share of them corre-
sponding to each disclosure type. For each group, we calculated

the values of the four predictors.
Each group thus became one observation, labeled with one of
the three disclosure types, and those items were used as training
and testing examples for the classifiers. Importantly, no scanpath
was used in both the training and testing of any classifier instance.

See Figure 3 for an illustration of the sampling and testing proce-
dure.

For each instance of a participant viewing a word grid, we measured the viewing
time, the number of words that were looked at, and the overall spatial gaze allocation,
particularly the tendency to look at positive vs. negative words. Most importantly, we
computed an index measuring the extent to which each scanpath was idiosyncratic vs.
typical. To this end, we calculated a matrix of pairwise spatio-temporal similarities
between all scanpaths, and then used a dimensionality-reduction algorithm to map the
scanpaths onto a plane in a way that approximates the similarities between them. We
further estimated the distribution of the obtained scanpath representation points.
Finally, we used a generalisation of the two-sided p-value to measure the extent to
which a given scanpath (or, more precisely, the point it was represented by) was
anomalous within the obtained distribution.
The above preprocessing pipeline is described in detail in the Appendix, and the
full code is available from the OSF project page. Results
We considered the impact of the disclosure on eye movements while viewing the
opinion word grid, and whether they can be used to infer the disclosure type. The data
and the preregistered analysis code are available via OSF (LINK).
Pilot study
For each trial, we calculated the average spatio-temporal similarity (see Cristino,
Mathôt, Theeuwes, & Gilchrist, 2010, and the Appendix) between the associated
eye-movement sequence (scanpath) and those of other participants from trials with the
same disclosure type (none, negative, or positive). We averaged this measure for each
participant-condition combination, obtaining three average similarity measures for each
participant. We found that the resulting between-subject-within-condition similarity for
no disclosure (Mdn=-0.299) was greater than for negative disclosure (Mdn=-0.356,
paired Wilcoxon two-tailed V=185, p=.002), but not significantly greater than for positive disclosure (Mdn=-0.308, V=148, p=.114). We based our preregistered sample
size rationale for the main study on the latter eﬀect, due to its smaller size.
Manipulation checks
We wished to verify that the participants understood the task and that its various
parameters had the desired eﬀect on decisions. Thus, we estimated a mixed-eﬀects
binary logistic regression with random subject intercept and slope eﬀects and the
investment decision as the dependent variable (1 = invest). Even in the no disclosure
condition, the adjustment was still revealed after viewing the word grid and could aﬀect
choice.
Hence, the independent variable set comprised two binary experimental condition
indicators (‘adjustment-disclosed’ and ‘adjustment-positive’), the interaction between
them, as well as a set of controls including the trial number, the proportion of positive
words in the grid, and the return obtained in the previous trial (motivated by the eﬀect
of past gains on subsequent risky choices, as reported by, e.g., Juechems, Balaguer,
Ruz, & Summerfield, 2017). Overall, when the adjustment was not disclosed prior to
seeing the word grid, the frequency of investment was smaller given a negative (delayed)
adjustment (57.5%) than for a positive one (69.9%,
βadjustment−positive = 0.617, p<.001). However, this eﬀect of a positive adjustment was
stronger (causing a change from 53.8% to 71.0%) when the adjustment was disclosed
beforehand rather than delayed (βadj.−disclosed ∗ adj.−pos. = 0.225, p=
.039).
Similarly, the control variable eﬀects were as expected, with the likelihood of
investment increasing with both the proportion of positive words in the grid
(βprop−positive = 3.060, p<.001) and the trial number (βtrial−number = 0.211, p=
.016).
Thus, participants were able to correctly recognize the words as positive or negative and
used them to inform their decisions. They were also apparently able to learn from the
fact that the eventual returns were, on average, significantly higher than the risk-free
return, and tended to invest more as the experiment progressed. At the same time, the
eﬀect of the previous trial return was not significant (βprev.−return = 0.046, p=
.753). [...]

The assumption that to-be-forgotten words are removed from
WM leads to two predictions: First, if to-be-forgotten information
is no longer in WM, it should be less accessible afterward. Hence,
performance in tests of to-be-forgotten items should be lower than
the to-be-remembered items of the same condition (directed-forgetting effects). Second, if information is removed from WM, it
should not interfere with the still relevant words, resulting in facilitation effects for the to-be-remembered information. Therefore,
performance for to-be-remembered words in the removal condition should be better than in the large set size baseline.

All analyses described below will be conducted using mixed-effects models in a Bayesian framework implemented in the R package brms (Bürkner, 2017), which provides an interface to Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017). Whenever not explicitly stated otherwise, the default settings of the brms package will be used. We will estimate the posteriors by sampling parameter values proportional to the product of prior and likelihood using the No-U-Turn Sampler in congestion with Hamilton Monte Carlo as implemented in Stan. We will sample generations through 4 independent Markov chains with 50,000 iterations each (2,000 warm up). To investigate convergence, we will inspect the Rhat values (<1.05 for all parameters). All categorical predictors will be coded as sum-to-zero contrasts. All continuous predictors will be mean-centered. 

For all models, the random effects structure for our design will include random intercepts for participants only. For all accuracy models, we will fit Bayesian generalized linear mixed models on the correctness of participants’ responses in a given trial assuming a Bernoulli data distribution predicted by a linear model through a logistic link function. For these models, we will give the regression coefficients moderately informative Cauchy priors with a scale of 0.353 (recently proposed default priors for logistic models; Oberauer, 2019).
For all models reported below, we will calculate Bayes Factors (BFs) to estimate the strength of evidence for the null and the alternative hypothesis. To this end, we will fit two competing, nested models for each hypothesis listed above; one including an effect (main effect or interaction) of interest and one that does not include this effect. We will then compare the two models to calculate the evidence for the effect. For the sakes of brevity, we will not always report both models but only the full model including all predictors of interest. 

T1, T2, T3 (exclusion of all set-size 6-3 forget trials and trials where the “new” word was selected as response): For the analyses of p(match|old), we will fit Bayesian generalized linear mixed models on the participants’ response correctness (1 = old-match word selected vs. 0 = old-mismatch word selected): One set of models will compare the set-size 6–X remember condition to the set-size 6 baseline (a); the other will compare the set-size 6–X remember condition to the set-size Y baseline (b). The models will include the fixed factors set-size (a: 6-X remember vs. 6; b: 6-X remember vs. Y) and SCI (T2: 0s vs 1s, T3: 1s vs 5s) as well as their interaction. To control for effects of learning and/or fatigue throughout the experiment, we will include the continuous predictor trial (trial number of a given trial) in our model. In addition, we will add the number of TBR items in a given trial (corresponding to 6-X and Y), thus the TBR set-size, as a predictor to our models. For T2 and T3, we will test whether a model including the interaction between set-size and SCI is superior to a model without that interaction. For T1, we will test whether a model including the factor set-size is superior to a model without that factor. Using pseudo-syntax as provided in brms, the fixed and random effect structure of the full models would be:
Correctness (match vs. mismatch) ~ set-size + SCI + trial + TBR set-size + set-size:SCI + (1|participant)

T4, T5 (set-size 6-3 forget trials only): To test whether the likelihood to select one of the old words over the new word [p(old)] in the 3AFC test differs between SCI levels, we will fit a Bayesian generalized linear mixed model on the participants’ responses (“old” vs. “new”) in a given TBF test trial. The model will include the fixed factor SCI (T4: 0s vs 1s; T5: 1s vs 5s). We will test whether a model containing the factor SCI is superior to a model without that factor:
Correctness (old vs. new) ~ SCI + (1|participant)

T6, T7 (set-size 6-3 forget trials only, exclusion of all trials where the “new” word was selected as response): To test whether the likelihood to select a match word over a mismatch word [p(match|old)] in the 3AFC test differs between SCI levels, we will fit a Bayesian generalized linear mixed model on the participants’ responses (“match” vs. “mismatch”) in a given TBF test trial. Taken together, Experiments 1–4 show robust directed-forgetting effects in WM. Yet, in all experiments, recognition performance of to-be-forgotten words was above chance level.

All analyses described below will be conducted using mixed-effects models in a Bayesian framework implemented in the R package brms (Bürkner, 2017), which provides an interface to Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017). The data analytic plan was preregistered, with four predictions
and several exploratory analyses. Our first prediction was that the
hedonic long-term goals (i.e., for increased positive affect and
decreased negative affect) would be the highest endorsed, consistent
with Study 1. To assess this, we calculated descriptive statistics on
the desired emotional self items (means, standard deviations) and we
calculated the percentage of people who selected each goal as a
“top” long-term emotional goal. Note that to fully explore the data,
consistent with our preregistration plan, we also conducted paired
samplest tests between the current emotional self ratings and desired
emotional self ratings with the assumption that most people would
consider their current emotional self less ideal/desirable than their
desired emotional self. We also calculated intergoal correlations
among the current emotional self items and the desired emotional
self items; these were exploratory and are available in Supplemental
Table S1.
1
Our second hypothesis was that greater discrepancies between
current emotional functioning (i.e., current emotional self) and the
desired emotional self would be associated with lower well-being.
To test this, we calculated difference scores by subtracting current
emotional self scores from desired emotional self scores, where
higher discrepancy scores reflect wanting the attribute more than
having it (Tamir et al., 2016). We calculated correlations between
the discrepancy scores and indicators of well-being—NA, PA, and
life satisfaction. Zero-order exploratory correlations between wellbeing indicators and the separate current emotional self attributes as
well as the long-term desired emotional self attributes are provided
in the Supplemental Materials to be fully transparent (Supplemental
Table S3).
Our third hypothesis was that people with greater positive affect
would report generally greater intention to work on emotional goals,
which we tested by correlating well-being indicators with the
average (across all 13 goals) intention to work toward long-term
emotional goals. Correlations between individual goal intentions
and indicators of well-being along with descriptive statistics for the
intention items are provided in Supplemental Table S4.
Finally, we wanted to confirm that people with lower well-being
tend to prioritize short-term over long-term emotional goals
(Christensen & Aldao, 2015). To assess this, we first conducted psychometric analyses on the eight items assessing attentiveness to
short- and long-term goals via a principal component analysis to
confirm that short- and long-term goal items loaded onto separate
factors (see Supplemental Table S5). We used an oblimin rotation,
as we did not want to assume these items were uncorrelated. We
calculated reliability ratings for the separate short- and long-term
goal scales and a difference score to reflect the relative degree
of attention to short- versus long-term goals. We then conducted
correlations between attentiveness to short-term, long-term, and
discrepancy between attentiveness to short- and long-term goals with
indicators of well-being and average current emotional self, desired
emotional self, and intention to work toward emotional goals.
In our preregistration plan, we also indicated an exploratory plan to
examine demographic differences, to assess the role of goal malleability
in long-term emotional goals, and to compare goals selected as “top”
with those not selected as “top” goals. To assess gender differences, we
calculated independent samples t tests comparing men and women on
the current emotional self (Supplemental Table S6) and the desired
emotional self (Supplemental Table S7). To assess goal malleability,
we first calculated descriptive statistics and correlations between goal
malleability and the other goal indicators (current emotional self,
desired emotional self, intention to work toward goals; Supplemental
Table S8). We originally preregistered an exploratory plan to assess
goal malleability as a potential mediator between desired emotional
goals and intention to work toward goals. However, as these data are
cross-sectional, we ultimately opted against mediation (Winer et al.,
2016), but we did conduct hierarchical regressions with the intention to
work toward each goal as the outcome variable. Step 1 had the current
emotional rating for that goal, Step 2 included the desire for that goal
long-term, and Step 3 had malleability for that goal. This analytic
method allowed for assessment of whether any relationship between
goal desire (Step 2) and intention to work decreased with the addition of
Step 3, thus providing a look at mediation with traditional methods, but
also allowed for a simpler examination of how each factor (current self,
desired self, malleability) contributes to goal intention. Notably,
because the individual analyses were similar across emotional goals,
we ultimately averaged across emotional attributes and present one
aggregated model (individual models are presented in Supplemental
Table S9).
To assess differences in the current emotional self, desired
emotional self, intention to work, and goal malleability on goals
selected as “top” versus those not selected as “top,” we first calculated
the number of “top” goals per person (between 0 and 4). We then
averaged ratings for the top goals ideographically per person and
averaged ratings for unselected goals in the same way. We calculated
paired samples t tests between the ratings for “top” and unselected
goals and present these in Supplemental Table S10.
The threshold for significance was preregistered as p < .01 due to
the number of exploratory analyses conducted.

paper_c2:
Data Analytic Plan
The data analytic plan was preregistered, with four predictions
and several exploratory analyses. Our rst prediction was that the
hedonic long-term goals (i.e., for increased positive affect and
decreased negative affect) would be the highest endorsed, consistent
with Study 1. To assess this, we calculated descriptive statistics on
the desired emotional self items (means, standard deviations) and we
calculated the percentage of people who selected each goal as a
“top” long-term emotional goal. Note that to fully explore the data,
consistent with our preregistration plan, we also conducted paired
samples t tests between the current emotional self ratings and desired
emotional self ratings with the assumption that most people would
consider their current emotional self less ideal/desirable than their
desired emotional self. We also calculated intergoal correlations
among the current emotional self items and the desired emotional
self items; these were exploratory and are available in Supplemental
Table S1.
1
Our second hypothesis was that greater discrepancies between
current emotional functioning (i.e., current emotional self) and the
desired emotional self would be associated with lower well-being.
To test this, we calculated difference scores by subtracting current
emotional self scores from desired emotional self scores, where
higher discrepancy scores re ect wanting the attribute more than
having it (Tamir et al., 2016). We calculated correlations between
the discrepancy scores and indicators of well-being—NA, PA, and
life satisfaction. Zero-order exploratory correlations between well-
being indicators and the separate current emotional self attributes as
well as the long-term desired emotional self attributes are provided
in the Supplemental Materials to be fully transparent (Supplemental
Table S3).
Our third hypothesis was that people with greater positive affect
would report generally greater intention to work on emotional goals,
which we tested by correlating well-being indicators with the
average (across all 13 goals) intention to work toward long-term
emotional goals. Correlations between individual goal intentions
and indicators of well-being along with descriptive statistics for the
intention items are provided in Supplemental Table S4.
Finally, we wanted to con rm that people with lower well-being
tend to prioritize short-term over long-term emotional goals
(Christensen & Aldao, 2015). To assess this, we rst conducted psychometric analyses on the eight items assessing attentiveness to
short- and long-term goals via a principal component analysis to
con rm that short- and long-term goal items loaded onto separate
factors (see Supplemental Table S5). We used an oblimin rotation,
as we did not want to assume these items were uncorrelated. We
calculated reliability ratings for the separate short- and long-term
goal scales and a difference score to re ect the relative degree
of attention to short- versus long-term goals. We then conducted
correlations between attentiveness to short-term, long-term, and
discrepancy between attentiveness to short- and long-term goals with
indicators of well-being and average current emotional self, desired
emotional self, and intention to work toward emotional goals.
In our preregistration plan, we also indicated an exploratory plan to
examine demographic differences, to assess the role of goal malleability
in long-term emotional goals, and to compare goals selected as“top”
with those not selected as“top” goals. To assess gender differences, we
calculated independent samples t tests comparing men and women on
the current emotional self (Supplemental Table S6) and the desired
emotional self (Supplemental Table S7). To assess goal malleability,
we rst calculated descriptive statistics and correlations between goal
malleability and the other goal indicators (current emotional self,
desired emotional self, intention to work toward goals; Supplemental
Table S8). We originally preregistered an exploratory plan to assess
goal malleability as a potential mediator between desired emotional
goals and intention to work toward goals. However, as these data are
cross-sectional, we ultimately opted against mediation (Winer et al.,
2016), but we did conduct hierarchical regressions with the intention to
work toward each goal as the outcome variable. Step 1 had the current
emotional rating for that goal, Step 2 included the desire for that goal
long-term, and Step 3 had malleability for that goal. This analytic
method allowed for assessment of whether any relationship between
goal desire (Step 2) and intention to work decreased with the addition of
Step 3, thus providing a look at mediation with traditional methods, but
also allowed for a simpler examination of how each factor (current self,
desired self, malleability) contributes to goal intention. Notably,
because the individual analyses were similar across emotional goals,
we ultimately averaged across emotional attributes and present one
aggregated model (individual models are presented in Supplemental
Table S9).
To assess differences in the current emotional self, desired
emotional self, intention to work, and goal malleability on goals
selected as“top” versus those not selected as“top,” we rst calculated
the number of“top” goals per person (between 0 and 4). We then
averaged ratings for the top goals ideographically per person and
averaged ratings for unselected goals in the same way. We calculated
paired samples t tests between the ratings for“top” and unselected
goals and present these in Supplemental Table S10.
The threshold for signi cance was preregistered as p < .01 due to
the number of exploratory analyses conducted.

paper_c1:
Based on the noisy-channel framework research, we make three
predictions. First, noncanonical sentences will be interpreted nonliterally more often than canonical sentences. This is because, for canonical sentences, the structural prior agrees with the grammatical
interpretation of the sentence, while, for noncanonical sentences, the
structural prior is at odds with the grammatical interpretation of the
sentence. Second, sentences where comprehenders assume deletions
will have the highest proportion of nonliteral interpretations, followed by insertions, followed by substitutions. Substitution edits
are predicted to be the least likely of the three because they assume
both that a chunk of the intended utterance was deleted and that an
unintended chunk was inserted in the perceived utterance; a substitution can be seen as a composition of a deletion and an insertion.
Note that the edits in question are not single-word edits (cf.,
Gibson et al., 2013) but changes in the suffix of the verb. This ordering is justified by Levenshtein distance and previous work with different types of edits, including edits to bound morphemes (Keshev &
Meltzer-Asscher, 2021; Zhan et al., 2017). Third, like Gibson et al.
(2013), we predict that ungrammatical fillers will result in a higher
rate of nonliteral interpretations in general. Following the likelihood
assumption in Bayesian reasoning, comprehenders rely more on
their world knowledge in noisy environments, regardless of whether
the experimental manipulation is to plausibility or the structure of the
sentence.

We will fit a Bayesian logistic regression model using the brms package in R. We will set literal interpretation to be the DV with canonicality and environment noise as IVs (main effects and interaction effect), with random intercepts for participants, verbs, with random slopes for environment noise within verbs. We will use a dynamical systems approach to examine competing ideas about how relationship expectations, perceptions of partner’s behaviours, and relationship quality (i.e., satisfaction, commitment, gratitude, and trust) influence each other from week to week during a relationship. All analyses will be two-level multilevel models conducted using the lme4 package (Bates, 2015) to account for the data’s nested structure. The three key weekly variables used in the primary model will be: 
1. Perceived Behaviours (positive and negative)
2. Forecasted Behaviours (positive and negative)
3. Relationship Quality (i.e., satisfaction, commitment, gratitude, and trust)

Positive versus negative behaviors will be tested in separate models, each including a separate relationship quality indicator. For example, one model will examine positive perceived behaviors, positive forecasted behaviors, and satisfaction from week to week. In total, we will conduct eight cross-lagged panel models in which each construct of interest – perceived behaviours, expected behaviours, and relationship quality – is modelled simultaneously as a predictor and as an outcome variable. “Last week” versions of each variable will be used as predictors (Time 1) and “this week” versions will be used as outcome variables (Time 2). Data will be restructured so that each of the three outcome variables – perceived behaviours, expected behaviours, and relationship quality at Time 2 – are combined into a single dependent variable column. Overall, each participant will have up to 12 rows in the data set: one for each dependent measure on each of the 4 weeks (Week 1 will be excluded because it will be missing “last week” variables). Three new dummy columns will be created to indicate which rows correspond to which DVs. The model will have a total of 12 predictors: each of the three dummy columns, plus each of the three dummy columns multiplied by each of the three Time 1 predictors. This analysis strategy will allow us to model all time change effects simultaneously in one model. Consistent with the theoretical outline provided above, we predict the following:

1. Relationship Quality (i.e., Satisfaction, Commitment, Gratitude, and Trust) (Time 1) will predict Forecasted Partner Behaviors (Time 2)
2. Forecasted Partner Behaviors (Time 1) will predict Perceived Partner Behaviors (Time 2)
