We will use R (R Core Team, 2021) and lme4 (Bates et al., 2012) to perform linear mixed effects analyses of the relationship between correct emotion categorization reaction times and errors, and perceiver and target factors. The model with the maximal random structure justified by the design included a five-way interaction between the five categorical variables of interest as well as random by-participant and by-item intercepts, random by-participant slopes for Target Sex, Target Race and Target Emotion, and random by-item slopes for Nationality Prime Condition and Perceiver Sex. Regression-style contrast coding (-.5 and .5 for the two levels of each variable, with reference levels determined alphabetically) will be used for all categorical variables. The bound optimization by quadratic approximation (bobyqa) with a set maximum of 200,000 iterations will be used. When convergence or singularity issues are encountered in the full model, the random effect structure will be simplified to the next best random effect structure (by iteratively removing random slopes for the variables that account for the smallest amount of variance). Including slopes for all variables resulted in singular fit convergence warnings, with the exception of by-participant slopes for Target Emotion. The most complex models would be:

lmer (RT ~ 1 + Nationality Prime * Perceiver Sex * Target Sex * Target Race * Target Emotion + (1 + Target Emotion * Target Sex * Target Race * Target Emotion |participant) + (1 + Nationality Prime * Perceiver Sex |item))

For female perceivers, there was evidence of a Target Sex × Target Emotion interaction (β = 27, t = 3.76, p < .001); pairwise comparisons indicated female perceivers showed a significant happy face advantage for female targets (Mdiff = 35 ms, 95% CI [23, 47], t = 6.60, p < .001) but not male targets (Mdiff = 8 ms, 95% CI [−4, 20], t = 1.52, p = .255). We further examined this interaction by running separate Target Sex × Target Emotion tests for each perceiver sex. For female perceivers, there was evidence of a Target Sex × Target Emotion interaction (β = .50, t = 2.77, p < .006); pairwise comparisons indicated that female perceivers showed a significant happy face advantage for female targets (OR = 1.53, 95% CI [1.12, 2.08], t = 3.07, p = .004) but showed no significant difference in either direction for male targets (OR = .93, 95% CI [.69, 1.25], t = .55, p = 1.00). Error data will be analysed using binomial general linear mixed effects regression (glmer), with Odds Ratios (OR)  described for the analyses and reported in Tables and proportion errors reported in Figures.

An OR is a measure of the likelihood of a particular outcome (see Szumilas, 2010). Where an OR equals 1, it indicates there is no difference in the likelihood of a particular outcome; thus, when lower and upper confidence intervals overlap 1 it indicates a null effect. When an OR is less than 1, it indicates a particular outcome is less likely to occur; thus, when lower and upper confidence intervals are both less than 1 it indicates an outcome is significantly less likely to occur. When an OR is greater than 1, it indicates a particular outcome is more likely to occur; thus, when lower and upper confidence intervals are both greater than 1 it indicates an outcome is significantly more likely to occur.

Outcome variables will be divided along 4 categories: well being, coping, symptoms, and individual measures. We will use a wide range of self-reported outcome measures to ensure reliable capture of change. Measures
Many of the explanatory and outcome variables in the study were

operationalized as preregistered composite measures, which were con-
structed using factor analysis via the “psych” package (Revelle, 2017).

For each composite variable, the adequacy of a single factor to sum-
marize the questionnaires used was confirmed using Horn’s Test of

Principal Components and applied to questionnaire scores using the
“paran” package (Dinno, 2012) in R.
Trait Measures: Across the Study Period
Trait measures were assessed via self-report questionnaires
administered at two-time points: baseline and postintervention.
We preregistered three planned composite outcome variables:
Well-being, Coping, and Symptom Burden. Composite scores
were created via the factor analysis function (fa) in R, which
gives standardized scores and is mean-centered. As Coping and
Symptom Burden were not the primary target outcome variables,

they are discussed in the online supplemental materials. Four mea-
sures were each operationalized using a single validated question-
naire: Stress Mindset, Mindfulness, Decentering, and Reappraisal.

Well-being. A composite of PA and life satisfaction, higher
scores indicated greater levels of subjective well-being (α = 0.82).
PANAS-Positive Affect
The PANAS (Watson et al., 1988) is a 20-item questionnaire that
measures PA and negative affect. The PA subscale, a 10-item measure indicating the extent to which an individual feels pleasant,
energetic, and concentrated, was used as the PA measurement for our
composed Well-being variable. Participants rated each item from 1
(very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely). Internal consistency
was good (α = 0.87) in our sample.
SWLS
The SWLS (Diener et al., 1985) is a five-item instrument
designed to measure people’s satisfaction with their lives and is

often used as a measure of the life satisfaction component of sub-
jective well-being. Participants rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to

7(strongly agree). Internal consistency was good (α = 0.85) in our
sample.
Stress Mindset. Stress mindset was assessed using the Stress
Mindset Measure (SMM; Crum et al., 2013), an eight-item measure

to address whether one person adopts a “stress-is-enhancing mind-
set” or “stress-is-debilitating mindset.” Participants rated each item

from 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Higher scores rep-
resented the mindset that stress is enhancing. Internal consistency for

the scale was good (α = 0.81).
Mindfulness. Mindfulness was assessed using the Five Facet
Mindfulness Questionnaire-15 (FFMQ-15; Baer et al., 2008),
which is a short form of the 39-item FFMQ measuring five
facets: Observing, Describing, Acting with Awareness,
Nonjudging, and Nonreactivity. Higher scores indicated better
mindfulness skills. Participants rated each item from 1 (never or

rarely true) to 5 (often or always true), with good internal consis-
tency (α = 0.81).

Decentering. Decentering was measured using the Metacogni-
tive Processes of Decentering-Trait (MPoD-t; Hanley et al., 2020),

which captures meta-awareness, (dis)identification with internal
experience, and (non)reactivity to internal experience. Participants
rated items from 1 (never or very rarely) to 5 (very often or always).

Higher scores indicated better decentering skills. Internal consis-
tency was good (α = 0.88).

Reappraisal. Reappraisal was measured using the Emotion
Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ; Gross & John, 2003). It includes
six items to assess the tendency to regulate emotions by cognitive
reappraisal (α = 0.82 in this sample). Statements investigated the
tendency to control or regulate emotion. Respondents answered

Primary hypothesis (hypothesis 1): We hypothesise that participants in the positive self-affirming AM condition will experience a greater intraindividual increase in momentary happiness from pre to post AM recollection compared to individuals in the neutral condition during the practice period. However, we expect an intraindividual reduction of sadness in both the positive and neutral AM conditions, since neutral AMs may have a distracting effect. 
We will assess whether this effect strengthens over the course of the training period, such that participants experience an increase in momentary emotional benefit following AM recollection in terms of (1) increased happiness and (2) decreased sadness over the course of the study. We will further determine whether momentary happiness and sadness are impacted by baseline wellbeing and depressive symptoms. 

Secondary hypothesis (hypothesis 2): We hypothesise that an independent set of 6 positive self-affirming AMs retrieved during the second laboratory session will on average be more positive in valence, more happy or satisfying upon recall, more vivid, and more self-concordant for individuals in the positive self-affirming AM condition (that is, that effects of training will generalise to positive memories that are not practiced) whereby controlling for the amount of practice with the diary.

Feasibility (hypothesis 3): In the follow-up period, we expect that individuals in the positive AM condition will use the AM diary more often spontaneously. We will explore whether this effect is stronger for those who experience a greater improvement in momentary happiness and greater decrease in momentary sadness during the training period (i.e., a moderation effect).

Exploratory: To determine the potential for a future relapse prevention study, we will explore whether the positive self-affirming AM group experiences an increase in wellbeing, relative to the neutral condition, from pre to post and follow-up assessments. We will also evaluate effects on residual depressive symptoms. We will further explore whether a potential increase in wellbeing and a decrease in depressive symptoms over the course of the study is mediated by the average experienced emotional benefits in happiness and sadness.

positive AMs would experience a greater intraindividual increase in
feelings of happiness from pre- to post-AM recollection, compared to
individuals in the everyday activity condition. We further expected an
intraindividual reduction of sadness in both the positive and everyday

hypothesis was that any benefits from the recollection of positive
AMs would generalize to untrained memories, such that following
study completion, participants in the positive AM condition would
more readily retrieve other, untrained positive AMs that were more

vivid, and more self-concordant relative to those in the everyday
activity condition. We also evaluated the potential of this technique
for reducing risk of depressive relapse. To index acceptability and
use, we hypothesized that individuals in the positive AM condition

anticipated this effect would be stronger for those who experienced a
greater improvement in feelings of happiness and a greater decrease in
feelings of sadness during training (third preregistered hypothesis).
To index potential effects on well-being, we explored whether those
in the positive condition experienced an increase in well-being and a
decrease in residual depressive symptoms from pre to post and to
follow-up assessments, relative to the everyday activity condition
(exploratory research question).

Memory Recollection and Recording
The digital AM diary started with a welcome screen, and
participants were asked to indicate whether they were making an
entry for training purposes or a spontaneous entry in response to a
low mood. They then indicated on a visual analog scale from 1 to 100
(not at all; extremely) the degree to which they felt four positively
(i.e., happy, interested, surprised, proud) and four negatively (i.e.,
scared, sad, upset, guilty) valenced affect terms. Their six preselected
AMs were then displayed, participants chose a memory to recall, and
they were subsequently presented with recollection instructions.
Both the positive and everyday activity conditions were instructed to
recollect their AM in a vivid and imagery-rich way, but only in the
positive condition were participants asked to focus on their positive emotions the memory elicited. Upon recollection of the memory,
participants worked through a series of prompts (see Supplemental
Figures S3 and S4) that guided them to experience their AMs in a
vivid (and, in the case of a positive AM, emotional) fashion. This
took approximately 3 min to complete, following which participants
rated AM vividness and AM-related imagery. Participants rated
positive AM vividness on a 5-point Likert scale (strongly disagree to
strongly agree) for three noninverse items taken from the Memory
Experiences Questionnaire (Sutin & Robins, 2007; my memory of the
event is very vivid; my memory of the event is very detailed; my
memory is very clear.) AM-related imagery was measured through
four items capturing different senses (i.e., see the memory with
your mind’s eye?/hear the memory with your mind’s ear?/smell
fragrances/feel physical sensations?; Slofstra et al., 2017), with
participants responding on a visual analog scale from 1 (not at all) to
5(completely). Afterward, participants rerated their experience of
each of the positive and negative emotions. The whole task took
approximately 5 min.
End-of-Day Questionnaire
Affect was assessed every evening with an adapted short form of
the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Thompson, 2007),
worded to assess average affect retrospectively over the course of
the day (for more details, see Supplemental Material S5).
Participants were then asked if they thought of any of the six
AMs at times when they were not keeping the diary. If they
answered in the affirmative, they were asked how often this was the
case and whether they thought of them deliberately or if they
appeared out of nowhere. If the participants thought of any of the
AMs deliberately, they were also asked if this was due to a low mood
and, if so, how often this was the case. A detailed overview on the
End-of-Day Questionnaire is provided in Supplemental Figure S6.
Participants were asked to complete the questionnaire at 7 p.m. Any
entries completed between 6 p.m. and 1 a.m. were included, and any
evening questionnaires that had been suspended for longer than
15 min were excluded.
Beck Depression Inventory–II (Beck et al., 1996)
The Beck Depression Inventory–II (BDI-II) is a 21-item selfreport measure assessing depressive symptoms over the previous
2 weeks. For each item, participants need to choose the statement
that best describes how they feel (e.g., “0 I do not feel sad; 1 I feel
sad; 2 I am sad all the time and I can’t snap out of it; 3 I am so sad and
unhappy that I can’t stand it”). Cronbach’s internal consistency was
high, α = 0.90 (95% CI [0.87, 0.94]).
The Short Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-Being
Scale (Tennant et al., 2007)
This self-report measure uses positively worded items to capture
different facets of positive mental health (e.g., “I’ve been feeling
optimistic about the future”; “I’ve been feeling useful”), which are
rated on a 5-point Likert scale (i.e., none of the time; rarely; some
of the time; often; all of the time). Again, Cronbach’s internal
consistency was high, α = 0.83 (95% CI [0.77, 0.9]).

paper_c2: Measures  Measures from the present study that were included in the analyses are detailed in the following section. Collected measures not included in the analyses are provided in Supplemental Material (S5).  Memory Recollection and Recording  The digital AM diary started with a welcome screen, and participants were asked to indicate whether they were making an entry for training purposes or a spontaneous entry in response to a low mood. They then indicated on a visual analog scale from 1 to 100 (not at all; extremely) the degree to which they felt four positively (i.e., happy, interested, surprised, proud) and four negatively (i.e., scared, sad, upset, guilty) valenced affect terms. Their six preselected AMs were then displayed, participants chose a memory to recall, and they were subsequently presented with recollection instructions. Both the positive and everyday activity conditions were instructed to recollect their AM in a vivid and imagery-rich way, but only in the positive condition were participants asked to focus on their positive emotions the memory elicited. Upon recollection of the memory, participants worked through a series of prompts (see Supplemental Figures S3 and S4) that guided them to experience their AMs in a vivid (and, in the case of a positive AM, emotional) fashion. This took approximately 3 min to complete, following which participants rated AM vividness and AM-related imagery. Participants rated positive AM vividness on a 5-point Likert scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree) for three noninverse items taken from the Memory Experiences Questionnaire (Sutin & Robins, 2007; my memory of the event is very vivid; my memory of the event is very detailed; my memory is very clear.) AM-related imagery was measured through four items capturing different senses (i.e., see the memory with your mind’s eye?/hear the memory with your mind’s ear?/smell fragrances/feel physical sensations?; Slofstra et al., 2017), with participants responding on a visual analog scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (completely). Afterward, participants rerated their experience of each of the positive and negative emotions. The whole task took approximately 5 min.  End-of-Day Questionnaire  Affect was assessed every evening with an adapted short form of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Thompson, 2007), worded to assess average affect retrospectively over the course of the day (for more details, see Supplemental Material S5). Participants were then asked if they thought of any of the six AMs at times when they were not keeping the diary. If they answered in the affirmative, they were asked how often this was the case and whether they thought of them deliberately or if they appeared out of nowhere. If the participants thought of any of the AMs deliberately, they were also asked if this was due to a low mood and, if so, how often this was the case. A detailed overview on the End-of-Day Questionnaire is provided in Supplemental Figure S6. Participants were asked to complete the questionnaire at 7 p.m. Any entries completed between 6 p.m. and 1 a.m. were included, and any evening questionnaires that had been suspended for longer than 15 min were excluded.  Beck Depression Inventory–II (Beck et al., 1996)  The Beck Depression Inventory–II (BDI-II) is a 21-item selfreport measure assessing depressive symptoms over the previous 2 weeks. For each item, participants need to choose the statement that best describes how they feel (e.g., “0 I do not feel sad; 1 I feel sad; 2 I am sad all the time and I can’t snap out of it; 3 I am so sad and unhappy that I can’t stand it”). Cronbach’s internal consistency was high, α = 0.90 (95% CI [0.87, 0.94]).  The Short Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale (Tennant et al., 2007)  This self-report measure uses positively worded items to capture different facets of positive mental health (e.g., “I’ve been feeling optimistic about the future”; “I’ve been feeling useful”), which are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (i.e., none of the time; rarely; some of the time; often; all of the time). Again, Cronbach’s internal consistency was high, α = 0.83 (95% CI [0.77, 0.9]).

Measures
In addition to the LWA Index (a = .95), Altemeyer’s RWA Scale
(a = .96), the Comprehensive Intellectual Humility Scale
(a = .89), Rokeach’s (Modified) Dogmatism Scale (a = .82), and the
previously described measures of partisan schadenfreude (a = .82),
partisan moral disengagement (a = .88), and partisan violence (a =
.86), participants completed measures of (a) autocratic/antidemocratic
orientation, (b) past use of force or violence for a political cause, (c)
desire to use force or violence for a political cause, (d) politically-motivated social media use, (e) willingness to sign petitions endorsing authoritarian political policies, (f) support for violent collective action
during protests in the summer of 2020, and (g) participation in violence during said protests.
Autocratic/Anti-Democratic Orientation. We administered
the Autocratic Orientation Scale (Bartusevicius et al., 2020), a
three-item measure of preferences for autocratic versus democratic
forms of governance. Participants with left-wing political views
were administered left-wing versions of the items, whereas individuals with right-wing political views were administered rightwing versions. The items were as follows: “Only [leftists/conservatives] are allowed to stand for election and hold office,”
“[Armed revolutionaries/the army] come[s] in to govern the country,” and “Elections and Congress are abolished so that a [leftist/
conservative] president can decide everything.” Response options
ranged from (1) Strongly disapprove to (7) Strongly approve. We
computed each participant’s total score over the three items
(higher values indicate a more autocratic orientation), M = 4.74,
SD = 2.75. Internal consistency was satisfactory for both left-wing
participants (a = .78) and right-wing participants (a = .78).
Political Social Media. Intolerance of difference is a fundamental component of authoritarianism (e.g., Stenner, 2009). As
such, highly authoritarian individuals should tend to prefer ideologically homogeneous social media environments. To test this hypothesis, we assessed the frequency with which participants had
blocked, unfriended or hidden someone on social media for (a)
posting too much political content, (b) posting political content
that participants disagreed with, (c) posting political content that
participants found offensive, (d) arguing about political issues
with participants or someone participants know, (e) disagreeing
with political content that participants posted, and (f) posting political content that participants worried would offend their friends or
people who follow them. Participants responded on a scale ranging from [0] Never to [3] Very Often. The six items (a = .88) were
averaged to yield a total score (M = .64, SD = .68).
Petitions in Support of Authoritarian Policies. Mocked-up
left- and right-wing versions of petitions in support of antidemocratic values (i.e., opposition to personal autonomy, individual
rights, and freedom of expression and belief) were administered to
participants. Participants were asked to sign two left-wing antidemocratic petitions and two right-wing antidemocratic petitions.
Response options ranged from [1] Definitely would not sign to [5]
Definitely would sign. The left-wing petitions were highly correlated (r = .60), as were the right-wing petitions (r = .53), so we
summed them to yield a left-wing petition score (M = 3.98,
SD = 2.03) and a right-wing petition score (M = 4.73, SD = 2.60).
Violent Protests. In May 2020, sweeping protests emerged
across more than 2,000 cities and towns in the United States in
response to the killings of George Floyd and other unarmed black
Americans by police officers and civilians. The protests included
mostly peaceful behavior, but they also included some violent protest behavior, such as burning police stations and cars, destroying
property, and throwing projectiles at police officers and political
opponents. Given that RWA and SDO predict prostate violence,
LWA should predict antistate violence (Webber et al., 2020).
Hence, the protests afforded an opportunity for a unique test of
LWA’s explanatory power for real-world behavior.
Attitudes. We constructed a nine-item measure of support
for violent aspects of the protests, with items ranging in severity from “Damaging property” to “Getting into physical fights
with political opponents.” Response options ranged from (1)
Completely oppose to (7) Completely support. Parallel analysis
favored a one-factor solution, which fit the data well, accounting for 81.1% of the total variance. The 9 items were a highly
internally consistent (a = .95) and were averaged to yield a total

The analysis will report:
- Zero-order correlations among all observed variables
- Descriptive statistics (N, Mean, Standard Deviation, Minimum, Maximum, Skew, Kurtosis) for all observed variables.

- Analysis of (correct) RTs in the attention capture task. We will specific a linear mixed model with trial-level RT data submitted to a model with fixed effects for distractor presence, sum-to-zero effects coded (1 = distractor-present, -1 = distractor-absent), and a random effect of participant (both intercept and slope allowed to vary). Then, in separate models, we will enter working memory capacity and attention control scores into the models as covariates, which are allowed to have both a main effect and an interactive effect with distractor presence. This will allow us to examine whether working memory capacity (WMC) and/or attention control (AC) affect overall RTs (significant main effect of score), whether they moderate the effect of target presence (significant score x distractor presence interaction), or both. Hypothesis 1 predicts WMC x distractor presence and AC x distractor presence interactions. Finally, we will enter WMC and AC into the model as covariates simultaneously to examine which factor drives the relations, if any. These analyses will be conducted using the lmerTest package in R.

Because there are so many oculometric indices extracted from the attention capture data, we will use a dimension reduction technique. Specifically, we will employ exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with the lavaan package in R. 

We expect there to be at least one coherent factor derived from the oculometric data, which will indicate visual search efficiency (e.g., longer time to fixate on target, more saccades on non-targets before target fixation) and/or overt visual attention capture by a singleton (proportion of distractor-present trials in which the singleton is fixated) Once these factors are identified, we will use the predict() function in lavaan to extract factor scores, and these will be correlated with the behavior indices of attention capture (Hypothesis 2) and the WMC and AC factor scores (Hypothesis 3). Finally, we will use multiple regression to examine the shared and unique influences of WMC and AC on the oculometrics. 

For the pupillary data, will compute the average change in pupil diameter to distractor-present and distractor-absent trials over the 1,500-ms window post stimulus onset. Then, these values will be correlated with the WMC and AC scores and the behavioral and oculometric attention capture measures (Hypothesis 4). Specifically, we hypothesize that larger pupillary responses will correlate with higher WMC, better AC, lower attention capture, and better visual search efficiency.

We will then compute the intraindividual mean and intraindividual standard deviation of pretrial pupil diameter for each participant, and this value will be correlated with the WMC and AC factor scores, the attention capture RT effect, and the oculometric factors (Hypothesis 5). Specifically, we hypothesize that less intraindividual variability in pretrial pupil diameter will correlate with higher WMC, better AC, lower attention capture, and better visual search efficiency.

Visual Search Task
Descriptive statistics for the dependent variables are listed in
Table 1, and zero-order correlations among the measures are listed
in Table 2. Disattenuated correlations can be found in Appendix
A. The results of a paired-samples t test demonstrated a significant
capture effect (mean difference = 173.52 ms) with a large effect
size, t(327) = 28.10, p , .001, d = 1.55, 95% confidence interval
[161.37, 185.67], BF10 . 100,000, such that participants had significantly longer RTs on distractor-present trials than on distractorabsent trials. Learning effects can be found in Appendix B, and
intertrial effects can be found in Appendix C.
Overall, participants who were more likely to fixate on the singleton
distractor at any given point within a trial (distraction probability) were
more likely to look at the distractor as the initial saccade of a trial
(r = .75, BF10 = 4.77). Those who took longer to initiate their first saccade were less likely to be distracted on the trial (distraction probability;
r =−.39, BF10 . 100,000), which could possibly be due to covertly
identifying the distractor prior to any movement and preventing a saccade to the distractor. Higher distraction probability was also associated
with a longer verification time (r = .20, BF10 = 8.52), such that those
who were more likely to have attention captured by the distractor took
longer to make a decision about the target. Not surprisingly, those who
were more likely to make a saccade to the distractor spent more time
fixating on the distractor (dwell time; r = .78, BF10 . 100,000).
Dwell time also correlated positively with verification time (r = .37,
BF10 . 100,000), such that those spending more time on the distractor
were slower to respond once identifying the target.
One interesting finding is that the RT effect (i.e., the difference in
RTs on distractor present and distractor absent trials) was not correlated with dwell time (r = .12, BF10 = 0.65), distraction probability
(r =−.04, BF10 = 0.19), or probability of the first saccade landing
on the distractor (r = .03, BF10 = 0.18). This is notable because the
RT effect is typically the dependent measure used for indicating attention capture. However, our eye-tracking results did not show that participants with a greater RT effect had higher probability of landing on
the distractor or spending more time fixated there. Therefore, overt
attentional capture measured via eye tracking did not have a
one-to-one relation, or even a particularly strong relation, with the
behavioral effect measured via RT. But, as demonstrated in Table 1,
the reliability of the RT capture effect is a meager .38, while the
oculometric-dependent variables’ reliabilities ranged from .79 to .97.
We also used a linear mixed model to estimate a capture effect for
each individual by allowing them to have random slopes and intercepts to better represent within-subject variability, which was exemplified by Roque (2018). This mixed model capture effect had higher
reliability than the subtraction method capture effect and was positively correlated with subtraction method capture effect (r = .60,
BF10 = .100,000), but the reliability was still not particularly
impressive (.68). The mixed model capture effect had more positive
correlations with the oculometric-dependent variables than the regular capture effect: those with greater capture as calculated by the
model had longer dwell time (r = .27, BF10 = 202.41), scan (r = .31,
BF10 = 2,026.94), verification times (r = .45, BF10 = .100,000),
and time to target (r = .38, BF10 = .100,000).
Factor Analysis
To examine whether the 10 oculometrics measured a smaller set of
dimensions, we submitted the variables to an exploratory factor analysis. The analysis yielded a solution with three factors with eigenvalues
. 1. However, this model did not fit well (comparative fit index = .97,
root mean square error of approximation = .13). Further, fitting the
suggested factor structure to a confirmatory factor analysis did not converge upon a solution. Therefore, we did not feel comfortable extracting and analyzing factor scores using this dimension-reduction
approach, and instead focus on individual oculometrics.
Attention Control and Working Memory Tasks
Our next of analyses examined whether the behavioral and oculometric measures of capture correlated with individual differences in
attention control and working memory capacity. Descriptive statistics for the attention control and working memory tasks are listed
in Table 3, and zero-order correlations among the measures are listed
in Table 4. Notably, the behavioral measures of the three attention
control tasks were highly reliable (..90) and significantly intercorrelated. The four working memory measures also significantly intercorrelated. Finally, z-score composites for attention control (average
of antisaccade, psychomotor vigilance task, and sustained attention
to cue task) and working memory capacity (average of operation
span, symmetry span, color change detection, and orientation
change detection) correlated significantly, r(367) = .35, p , .001,
BF10 . 100,000. Thus, our chosen measures of attention control
and working memory showed coherent psychometrics.
Correlations among the attention capture oculometrics and the
working memory and attention control composites are found in
Table 5. Behaviorally, working memory capacity (but not attention
control) was modestly but significantly correlated with higher accuracy (r = .19, BF10 = 28.15), and both working memory (r =−.24,
BF10 = 837.25) and attention control (r =−.37, BF10 . 100,000)
were correlated with faster RTs on the visual search task. The subtraction method RT capture effect (difference between distractorpresent and distractor-absent trials) was not correlated with working
memory capacity (r =−.09, BF10 = 0.48) or attention control (r =
−.06, BF10 = 0.21). We also refit the linear mixed model with
working memory capacity and attention control as covariates in the
model. The model including working memory capacity yielded a
significant main effect of working memory (b =−212.50, SE =
83.28, p = .011), but a Nonsignificant Working Memory × TrialType interaction (b =−61.60, SE = 37.89, p = .105). The model
including attention control yielded a significant main effect of attention control (b =−433.52, SE = 73.19, p , .001), but a
Nonsignificant Attention Control × Trial-Type interaction (b =
11.37, SE = 34.89, p = .745).4 Thus, people who were better at
the attention control and working memory tasks were overall faster
at responding on the visual search task.
With the oculometrics, there were scant significant correlations.
Dwell time and verification time negatively correlated with working
memory (dwell time: r =−.22, BF10 = 23.40; verification time: r =
−.31, BF10 = 3,670.40) and attention control (dwell time: r =−.24,
BF10 = 79.20; verification time: r =−.30, BF10 = 2,017.33), such
that those spending less time fixated on the distractor, and making a
response decision scored higher on working memory and attention
control. Neither average task-evoked pupillary responses (attentional
intensity) nor intraindividual variability in pretrial pupil diameter
(attentional consistency) were correlated with working memory capacity or attention control. Notably, the lack of correlations here could not
be attributed to a lack of reliability in the metrics (see Table 1).

Procedure
We used an experimental procedure that was shown to effectively
mask the real purpose of the experiment and thereby reduces the influence of demand characteristics (Figure 2). Moreover, as shown by
Givon et al. (2020), this procedure elicits genuinely felt emotions
rather than reports of expected emotion (see Itkes et al., 2017). Participants (N = 34) performed two tasks: a (focal) emotion task and a perceptual task with trials of the two tasks interleaved. The perceptual
task served to disguise the real purpose of the experiment; we told
participants that we were exploring how their emotions influence their
performance in a pure perceptual task. Additionally, the perceptual
task minimized a carryover effect of emotion from previous trials.
Finally, we planned to use the perceptual task as a validated reference
point to the emotion task (in retrospect, the circle task was not a valid
reference point to the emotion task since in tasks that involve comparison to a standard, evidence accumulation models are not suitable to
detect Weber’s law [Ratcliff et al., 2018]. Therefore, we will not
report the circle task results in the main text, but the rest of the information regarding the method and results of the circle task can be
found in the online supplemental materials).
The Emotion Task
The most important are trials of the emotion task (Figure 2a), in
which we presented participants with normed emotion-eliciting
pictures (from the Nencki Affective Picture System, or NAPS;
Marchewka et al., 2014) and asked them to report whether the picture makes them feel pleasant or unpleasant. Responses were
made by pressing one of two keys, while their responses and their
RTs were recorded. The emotion-eliciting pictures belonged to six
valence categories, being around 2, 3, or 4 (negative) and 6, 7, or 8
(positive) on a 1–9 scale.
The Perceptual Task
In trials of the perceptual task (Figure 2b), participants were
introduced to a standard circle with a fixed-size diameter (225 pixels), and their task was to determine whether the next circle
presented to them was larger or smaller than the standard circle.
There were four circles that were larger than the standard circle
and four that were smaller than it. Each circle area was 5% larger/
smaller than its previous circle in the series.
Since this experiment was conducted during COVID-19, participants performed the experiment using their own personal laptop at
their own homes. Given this fact and in order to keep the participants
committed and engaged as well as to check their well-being during
the experiment, participants were connected with the experimenter
using a Zoom video call throughout the experiment and opened their
camera and microphone between blocks to allow the experimenter to
get an impression of their well-being and engagement in the task.
After participants performed the tasks (Figure 2), we sent them a
link to a video believed to induce inspiration and positive mood and
asked them to answer some questions related to this video. The purpose of the video was to dilute the effect of the difficult-to-view
images so that the participants would leave the experiment in a mood
as positive as possible. For the same reason, the experiment contained more positive than negative emotional stimuli.

In this study we will use the method of fitting a hierarchical Bayesian evidence-accumulation model. This hierarchical method estimates parameters for each individual separately, but constrain these estimations with the population distribution (see Lin & Strickland, in press, Appendix, for details).

Follow-up analyses

In this study we will use a method of model comparison to test some of our hypothesis. The fundamental idea in this method is to fit several different LBA models, and to decide which model fits the data best. To do so, we will create the null model (M1) with all its parameters set to be equal across different levels of the dependent variable in question. Then, we will create five more models (M2-M6), which in every one of those models a different parameter will set as a function of the dependent variable. The null model will serve as a comparison model to the other models. 

Because hierarchical modeling is a time-consuming process, we will use hierarchical modeling only for our main hypotheses. In addition, in order to interpret the data obtained from the hierarchical analysis, the Gelman-Robin index for each individual and for all subjects together must be less than 1.1. If we won't meet this requirement, or if the hypotheses under examination is not a main hypothesis, we will use simpler methods for estimating the model parameters. The simpler method treats the data as if they came from "one big subject".  This approach is based on maximum likelihood estimation, and issues BIC values for comparative model fit assessment. This method will conduct using 'rtdists' or 'glba' R packages.  Any model that will have a significant smaller DIC or BIC then M1, will account as a model that fit the data the best. This method will be used by us in the analyses of few of our hypothesis.

To test our hypothesis that emotional awareness obeys Weber's law, we first need to show that the LBA model is suitable to find evidence to Weber’s law even for physical stimuli. We thus intend to show that the LBA model can detect Weber's law for the perception of circle size. We term the related hypothesis “tool-validity hypothesis” (TVH) to mark the fact that it is not a core hypothesis. To do so, we will use the model comparison method, and fit several different LBA models to circle responses. Model 1 (TVH-M1) is the null model with all its parameters set to be equal across different levels of the circle size. In Model 2 (TVH-M2), DR is a function of circle size. In model 3 (TVH-M3), SV will set as a function of the circle size. We expect that in TVH-M7, SV will increase linearly with stimulus intensity, while DR will increase as the circle size move farther away from the target circle. If TVH-M7 is shown to be superior over TVH-M2 and TVH-M3, this will support our prediction. In every one of the four remaining models (TVH-M4- TVH-M6), a different parameter (SP, non-decision, b) will set as a function of the different levels of the circle size. We will choose the best model to fit the data, based on the DIC or BIC differences between the models (significantly smallest DIC/BIC).  

In a case that less than 75% of the subjects will fit more to one model compared to the other model (can be deduced by the DIC differences for each subject in both models), we will perform another analysis. For this analysis we will randomly split the data into two separate data sets, so that each subject's trials will be equally distributed between the two sets of data. We than re-run the model with both new data sets, and examined whether the percentage of subjects to fit one model compared to the other model remain almost the same. If the percentage will remain quite like the percentages of the first analysis, we can conclude that the differences between both models are not coincidental. 

If our hypothesis is not supported by the data, we have two options: First, the LBA model is not suitable to express Weber's law. The second option is that something in the experimental procedure went wrong, then we can fix it and try again. Importantly, until (or whether) the tool-validity hypothesis is supported is a pre-requisite for testing the core hypothesis which is described next. 

In order to test our core hypothesis (that emotional awareness obey Weber's law), we will compare between several alternative models which are strictly analogous to the models we have described above, except for being applied to (un) pleasantness reports. 

The circle task is used for two purposes: (1) to create a validated reference-point to the emotional and gamble tasks. (2) To function as a disguise (subjects will be led to believe that we are examining whether emotional stimulation/ gamble outcomes affect perception of circles area). In order to create a validated reference-point, we will use the method of model comparison as described above, and apply it on the difference between tasks (circle, emotional). We expect to find that the model that will show to be superior to the other models, is the model that allows the SP parameter to vary between tasks. This hypothesis is in accordance with previous work conducted in our lab (Givon et al., 2019). 

We would also like to check for selective influence as means to validate the model and to replicate prior similar validation by Givon et al. (2019). To do so, we will once again use the method of model comparison, and compare between different levels of some of the depended variables (circle size, intensity, valance). We believe that the model that will have the smallest BIC for each of those variables, will be the model that allows the DR and the SV parameters to vary between different levels of the depended variables. If this prediction will be supported, this will serve as evidence for selective influence. As sanity check, we would also aspect to receive higher drift-rate for negative feeling, then for positive felling (as was found in previous work conducted in our lab).

In this experiment, we will use the DR parameter, per emotional intensity photo, in order to put the emotional stimuli trials on a ratio scale. This will be possible if indeed the DR parameter will increase as the circle size move farther away from the target circle.


The evidence-accumulation model that we will use is the liner ballistic accumulation model (LBA). In its more standard applications, this model contains of five parameters: drift rate (v), the drift rate standard deviation (SV), non-decision time, starting point (SP) and response threshold (b) (St0- the range of non-decision time, is usually fixed at zero, since adding it to the model substantially increases fitting time, and since usually there is no substantial question that relates to it).

Model Fitting
For modeling purposes, we defined correct and wrong emotion
reports according to adherence to norms, an assumption justified by
the fact that aberrant emotion reports have been shown to be processed similarly to aberrant perceptual decisions—that is, errors
(Givon et al., 2022), most importantly in terms of aberrant RT distributions being relatively more right skewed but also in terms of
speed-accuracy trade-off, post-error slowing, and electroencephalogram error-related negativity. We estimated the LBA parameters for
each individual, using Bayesian hierarchical modeling (ggdmc R
package; Lin & Strickland, 2020). Modeling allowed us to estimate
DR for the accumulator generating normative (“correct”) responses
and for the accumulator generating normatively aberrant (“wrong”)
responses, separately. To test our main hypotheses,1 we fit two different models (Figures 3 and 4): M-P, a model with which we estimated DR and SV for the accumulator representing “pleasant,” and
M-N, a model with which we estimated DR and SV for the accumulator representing “unpleasant.” Specifically, in M-P, DR and SV of
“pleasant” were free parameters. These include the parameters of
the normative “pleasant” responses to normatively positive stimuli,
a pair of DR and SV parameters for each one of the three intensity
levels 6, 7, and 8. It also included the parameters representing
the accumulator generating normatively aberrant “pleasant”
responses to normatively negative stimuli (intensity levels 2, 3,
4). The rest of the parameters were fixed to reduce model complexity, thereby improving parameter estimation. All these fixed parameters were set to be equal to the values that were estimated in
the null model, in which emotion intensity was disregarded. These
fixed values included nondecision time (t0), range of evidence present in the accumulator before evidence accumulation begins (A),
the amount of evidence needed to be gathered in order to cross a
boundary and reach a decision (B), and, most importantly, DR for
the “correct” (normative) and “incorrect” (aberrant) accumulator.
SV was 1.0 for all the unpleasant conditions and thus defined the
unit. We used one set of priors for the null model and another set of
priors for the rest of the models. Specifically, the mean priors for
the null model were A = 2, B = 2, t0 = .3, DR.true = 2, and
DR.false = .5 (“false” and “true,” indicating whether it was the accumulator generating the normative response or the aberrant
response, respectively), while SV = 1 sets the scaling. After creating
the null model, we used its estimates of posteriors in specifying the
core models, M-P and M-N. Specifically, the estimated (across participants) mean posterior parameter values obtained from the null
model were used to create priors and fixed values for the parameters
in M-P and M-N. These included specific DR and SV parameters,
depending on whether it was M-P or M-N. Additionally, the (across
participants) mean posterior parameter values from the null model
were used as fixed A, B, and t0 values in M-N and M-P. The same
(but reversed) logic was applied in M-N. In summary, in each M-P
and M-N, we assessed DR and SV in a different accumulator, with
M-P used to assess these parameters for the accumulator generating
“pleasant” responses and with M-N doing the same for the accumulator generating “unpleasant” responses (see Figure 3).
Hierarchical Bayesian modeling involves computing posterior
probability distributions for each parameter based on the priors and
the data. For all models, the priors for DR (and SV) were the same
across all valence levels, meaning that any difference between posterior parameter estimates could not have been caused by the priors.
In detail, the model computes posterior probability by sampling
from the space of all possible parameter value combinations, and this
sampling is accomplished with the Markov chain Monte Carlo
(MCMC) method. MCMC produces chains of samples and is accomplished in two steps: The first step is an initial “burn-in” period that
tunes the chains to regions in the parameter space with values associated with nonnegligible posterior probability. The initial burn in is
then followed by the second step, which is the actual sampling of
posteriors. For each model, the sampling started with 1,000 burn-in
samples per chain, with a default number of parallel chains that determine 3 times the number of free parameters in the model. For the
actual sampling, we used the same default number of chains, with
8,000 samples per chain and thinning = 12 (keep each 12th sample).
We assessed the sampling adequacy of the posteriors using the
potential scale reduction factor (PSRF). PSRF is the ratio between
the within-chain variance and the between-chain variance, and it is
argued that the MCMC chains are well converged when PSRF is
less than 1.1 (Brooks & Gelman, 1998; Schubert et al., 2017).
Finally, we used Bayesian repeated-measures analysis of variance
with default priors to compute Bayes factors (BF10; the relative
posterior odds of H1 relative to H0) of the predicted effects and
used visual inspection to test the directionality of the posteriors.
Results
For all the participants in the null model, M-P and M-N, PSRF
fell considerably below 1.1, with the highest PSRF being 1.044,
suggesting the model’s estimates of posteriors are trustworthy. We
additionally assessed absolute model fit using the root mean square
error of approximation (RMSEA; Steiger & Lind, 1980), which
has been extended to evidence accumulation modeling by Schubert et al. (2017).
2 The 95% confidence interval (CI) for
RMSEA was computed using bootstrap (number of samples =
500), with resampling conducted over participants. According to
Schubert et al., RMSEA , .08 indicates good fit. For the null
model, M-P and M-N, RMSEA fell below .05, which indicates a
good model fit (RMSEA = .012, 95% CI [.009, .014]; RMSEA =
.038, [.036, .04]; RMSE = .013, [.011, .015], respectively). We
additionally compared the RMSEA values obtained for the emotion task to those of the circle task. This comparison was possible
since we used similar logic to the one used to build M-P and M-N,
resulting in three models: the null model, M-B (a model for “bigger” accumulator), and M-S (a model for the “smaller” accumulator). For the null model, M-B and M-S, RMSEA fell below .05
(RMSE = .000, [.000, .000]; RMSE = .041, [.038, .044]; RMSE =
.043, [.04, .047], respectively). It seems that the circle task null
model is a better fit than the emotion null model, but when comparing the rest of the models, overall, it seems that the modeling emotion reports shows a better fit to the data as compared to the circle
task. These results suggest that using the LBA to model emotional
reports is as justified as using the LBA to model perceptual decisions, which are its “comfort zone,” so to speak. More information
regarding the modeling of the circle task can be found in the online
supplemental materials. We may add that the legitimacy of using
the LBA to model emotion reports is additionally gained from other
studies (Givon et al., 2020; Singer-Landau & Meiran, 2021) where
critical components of model validation were included, including
comparison to alternative models and showing selective influence
of manipulations on the predicted LBA parameters.
Testing P1
Once we established the legitimacy of the LBA as a model of
the current results, we could move to testing the core predictions.
For M-P, we found that as valence became less negative and more
positive, DR increased (BF10 = 4.943e þ 81; Figure 5a). For M-N,
we found that as valence became less negative and more positive,
the DR decreased (BF10 = 1.327e þ 76; Figure 5a). These results
support P1 since DR changed monotonically with the picture
norms and given that DR = M(drift rate). This result allows us to
consider drift rate as a ratio scale for emotion intensity.

Regarding P2, for both M-P and M-N, we found that as stimuli
become less negative and more positive, SV increased (BF10 =
1.643e þ 31; BF10 = 120,606.191, respectively; Figure 5b). This
finding suggests that, as predicted, the experience of pleasant emotion obeys Weber’s law, indicating reduced encoding precision

pictures’ normative ratings, as shown in Figure 5c.

Statistical models
In this study we will use the method of fitting a hierarchical Bayesian evidence-accumulation model. This hierarchical method estimates parameters for each individual separately, but constrain these estimations with the population distribution (see Lin & Strickland, in press, Appendix, for details).

Follow-up analyses

In this study we will use a method of model comparison to test some of our hypothesis. The fundamental idea in this method is to fit several different LBA models, and to decide which model fits the data best. To do so, we will create the null model (M1) with all its parameters set to be equal across different levels of the dependent variable in question. Then, we will create five more models (M2-M6), which in every one of those models a different parameter will set as a function of the dependent variable. The null model will serve as a comparison model to the other models. 

Because hierarchical modeling is a time-consuming process, we will use hierarchical modeling only for our main hypotheses. In addition, in order to interpret the data obtained from the hierarchical analysis, the Gelman-Robin index for each individual and for all subjects together must be less than 1.1. If we won't meet this requirement, or if the hypotheses under examination is not a main hypothesis, we will use simpler methods for estimating the model parameters. The simpler method treats the data as if they came from "one big subject".  This approach is based on maximum likelihood estimation, and issues BIC values for comparative model fit assessment. This method will conduct using 'rtdists' or 'glba' R packages.  Any model that will have a significant smaller DIC or BIC then M1, will account as a model that fit the data the best. This method will be used by us in the analyses of few of our hypothesis.

To test our hypothesis that emotional awareness obeys Weber's law, we first need to show that the LBA model is suitable to find evidence to Weber’s law even for physical stimuli. We thus intend to show that the LBA model can detect Weber's law for the perception of circle size. We term the related hypothesis “tool-validity hypothesis” (TVH) to mark the fact that it is not a core hypothesis. To do so, we will use the model comparison method, and fit several different LBA models to circle responses. Model 1 (TVH-M1) is the null model with all its parameters set to be equal across different levels of the circle size. In Model 2 (TVH-M2), DR is a function of circle size. In model 3 (TVH-M3), SV will set as a function of the circle size. We expect that in TVH-M7, SV will increase linearly with stimulus intensity, while DR will increase as the circle size move farther away from the target circle. If TVH-M7 is shown to be superior over TVH-M2 and TVH-M3, this will support our prediction. In every one of the four remaining models (TVH-M4- TVH-M6), a different parameter (SP, non-decision, b) will set as a function of the different levels of the circle size. We will choose the best model to fit the data, based on the DIC or BIC differences between the models (significantly smallest DIC/BIC).  

In a case that less than 75% of the subjects will fit more to one model compared to the other model (can be deduced by the DIC differences for each subject in both models), we will perform another analysis. For this analysis we will randomly split the data into two separate data sets, so that each subject's trials will be equally distributed between the two sets of data. We than re-run the model with both new data sets, and examined whether the percentage of subjects to fit one model compared to the other model remain almost the same. If the percentage will remain quite like the percentages of the first analysis, we can conclude that the differences between both models are not coincidental. 

If our hypothesis is not supported by the data, we have two options: First, the LBA model is not suitable to express Weber's law. The second option is that something in the experimental procedure went wrong, then we can fix it and try again. Importantly, until (or whether) the tool-validity hypothesis is supported is a pre-requisite for testing the core hypothesis which is described next. 

In order to test our core hypothesis (that emotional awareness obey Weber's law), we will compare between several alternative models which are strictly analogous to the models we have described above, except for being applied to (un) pleasantness reports. 

The circle task is used for two purposes: (1) to create a validated reference-point to the emotional and gamble tasks. (2) To function as a disguise (subjects will be led to believe that we are examining whether emotional stimulation/ gamble outcomes affect perception of circles area). In order to create a validated reference-point, we will use the method of model comparison as described above, and apply it on the difference between tasks (circle, emotional). We expect to find that the model that will show to be superior to the other models, is the model that allows the SP parameter to vary between tasks. This hypothesis is in accordance with previous work conducted in our lab (Givon et al., 2019). 

We would also like to check for selective influence as means to validate the model and to replicate prior similar validation by Givon et al. (2019). To do so, we will once again use the method of model comparison, and compare between different levels of some of the depended variables (circle size, intensity, valance). We believe that the model that will have the smallest BIC for each of those variables, will be the model that allows the DR and the SV parameters to vary between different levels of the depended variables. If this prediction will be supported, this will serve as evidence for selective influence. As sanity check, we would also aspect to receive higher drift-rate for negative feeling, then for positive felling (as was found in previous work conducted in our lab).

In this experiment, we will use the DR parameter, per emotional intensity photo, in order to put the emotional stimuli trials on a ratio scale. This will be possible if indeed the DR parameter will increase as the circle size move farther away from the target circle.


The evidence-accumulation model that we will use is the liner ballistic accumulation model (LBA). In its more standard applications, this model contains of five parameters: drift rate (v), the drift rate standard deviation (SV), non-decision time, starting point (SP) and response threshold (b) (St0- the range of non-decision time, is usually fixed at zero, since adding it to the model substantially increases fitting time, and since usually there is no substantial question that relates to it).

[...]

Inference criteria
We intend to employ hierarchical Bayesian estimation (as instantiated in the ‘ggdmc’ R-package). This estimation method yields DIC estimated per subject. Thus, for each subject, we will determine which model fits the data the best (lowest DIC). We will use Bayesian Binomial test to compare subjects DIC score that obtained from different models, in order to show that one model in superior to the other not just by chance. 

For the simpler methods for estimating the model parameters, we will use Bayes Factor (BF) to determine which of the models fit the data the best. In order to calculate BF, we will use this function BF = e0.5*ΔBIC.  We will treat the results as significant when BF will be greater than 5.

We estimated the LBA parameters for
each individual, using Bayesian hierarchical modeling (ggdmc R
package; Lin & Strickland, 2020). Modeling allowed us to estimate
DR for the accumulator generating normative (“correct”) responses
and for the accumulator generating normatively aberrant (“wrong”)
responses, separately. To test our main hypotheses,1 we fit two different models (Figures 3 and 4): M-P, a model with which we estimated DR and SV for the accumulator representing “pleasant,” and
M-N, a model with which we estimated DR and SV for the accumulator representing “unpleasant.” Specifically, in M-P, DR and SV of
“pleasant” were free parameters. These include the parameters of
the normative “pleasant” responses to normatively positive stimuli,
a pair of DR and SV parameters for each one of the three intensity
levels 6, 7, and 8. It also included the parameters representing
the accumulator generating normatively aberrant “pleasant”
responses to normatively negative stimuli (intensity levels 2, 3,
4). The rest of the parameters were fixed to reduce model complexity, thereby improving parameter estimation. All these fixed parameters were set to be equal to the values that were estimated in
the null model, in which emotion intensity was disregarded. These
fixed values included nondecision time (t0), range of evidence present in the accumulator before evidence accumulation begins (A),
the amount of evidence needed to be gathered in order to cross a
boundary and reach a decision (B), and, most importantly, DR for
the “correct” (normative) and “incorrect” (aberrant) accumulator.
SV was 1.0 for all the unpleasant conditions and thus defined the
unit. We used one set of priors for the null model and another set of
priors for the rest of the models. Specifically, the mean priors for
the null model were A = 2, B = 2, t0 = .3, DR.true = 2, and
DR.false = .5 (“false” and “true,” indicating whether it was the accumulator generating the normative response or the aberrant
response, respectively), while SV = 1 sets the scaling. After creating
the null model, we used its estimates of posteriors in specifying the
core models, M-P and M-N. Specifically, the estimated (across participants) mean posterior parameter values obtained from the null
model were used to create priors and fixed values for the parameters
in M-P and M-N. These included specific DR and SV parameters,
depending on whether it was M-P or M-N. Additionally, the (across
participants) mean posterior parameter values from the null model
were used as fixed A, B, and t0 values in M-N and M-P. The same
(but reversed) logic was applied in M-N. In summary, in each M-P
and M-N, we assessed DR and SV in a different accumulator, with
M-P used to assess these parameters for the accumulator generating
“pleasant” responses and with M-N doing the same for the accumulator generating “unpleasant” responses (see Figure 3).
Hierarchical Bayesian modeling involves computing posterior
probability distributions for each parameter based on the priors and
the data. For all models, the priors for DR (and SV) were the same
across all valence levels, meaning that any difference between posterior parameter estimates could not have been caused by the priors.
In detail, the model computes posterior probability by sampling
from the space of all possible parameter value combinations, and this
sampling is accomplished with the Markov chain Monte Carlo
(MCMC) method. MCMC produces chains of samples and is accomplished in two steps: The first step is an initial “burn-in” period that
tunes the chains to regions in the parameter space with values associated with nonnegligible posterior probability. The initial burn in is
then followed by the second step, which is the actual sampling of
posteriors. For each model, the sampling started with 1,000 burn-in
samples per chain, with a default number of parallel chains that determine 3 times the number of free parameters in the model. For the
actual sampling, we used the same default number of chains, with
8,000 samples per chain and thinning = 12 (keep each 12th sample).
We assessed the sampling adequacy of the posteriors using the
potential scale reduction factor (PSRF). PSRF is the ratio between
the within-chain variance and the between-chain variance, and it is
argued that the MCMC chains are well converged when PSRF is
less than 1.1 (Brooks & Gelman, 1998; Schubert et al., 2017).
Finally, we used Bayesian repeated-measures analysis of variance
with default priors to compute Bayes factors (BF10; the relative
posterior odds of H1 relative to H0) of the predicted effects and
used visual inspection to test the directionality of the posteriors.

Based on the findings of Marks (1987), we conjecture the following:
(1) Human performance in the brightness classification task should depend upon whether there is a match or a mismatch between the visual target brightness and auditory distractor loudness. That is to say, responses to a bright (dim) visual target should on average be faster and more accurate when the simultaneously presented auditory distractor is loud (soft) than when it is soft (loud). This hypothesis will be tested with two ANOVAs performed separately on the mean response time (RT) and response accuracy data from the brightness classification task. This crossmodal correspondence between brightness and loudness should be reflected in both of the ANOVAs as a statistically reliable interaction effect between the two nominal predictors “brightness” and “loudness”.

(2) Performance in the lightness classification task should on the other hand be independent of the intensity pairing between the visual target and the distractor tone. We therefore expect no Lightness × Loudness interaction in the analysis of the lightness classification data. Testing this hypothesis will involve two separate ANOVAs to be performed on the mean RT and error rates from the lightness classification.

(3) As implied by hypotheses (1) and (2), joint ANOVAs conducted on the combined data from the lightness and brightness classification tasks should further reveal Mode × Visual Intensity × Auditory Intensity interaction effects for both the speed and accuracy of performance. That is, there should be a statistically reliable three-way interaction effect between the mode of visual appearance (brightness/lightness), the intensity of the visual signal and the loudness of the auditory distractor on both RT and accuracy of performance. 

(4) A within-subjects t-test will be performed on RT and accuracy rates from matching vs mismatching trials types to confirm that the crossmodal correspondence interaction effects are in the expected direction (i.e., faster and more accurate performance on matching type trials).

We used 24 videos of actors performing everyday activities.
Spatial location varied between the videos and showed actors performing activities inside (e.g., baking) and outside (e.g., washing
car). Six of the video clips were recut from videos used by BenYakov et al. (2021) the remaining 18 were shot by one of the authors
(Dominika Varga). The video clips were stop-motion presenting six
frames per second and had a mean length of 29.87 (+8.74; range
= 18.14–53.6).
For each video clip, we created two versions that manipulated the
information presented in them. Unlike Experiments 1–3, here we
maintained the length of the video clips under different conditions.
This was done by using a sliding window approach, such that videos
in the incomplete condition started earlier than videos in the updated
condition. The videos were cut to end before or shortly after an
action was completed. We selected videos that had an additional
scene change after the last action in the first scene was completed
and would show the start of a new event. On average the duration
of the new event after the scene change (e.g., wiping the forehead)
was 1.99 (+0.57) s. On average, the incomplete video clips were
shifted 4.96 (+1.08) s forward in time to include the completed
action, the scene change, and the short event after the boundary.
We varied which videos are in the incomplete condition and
which were in the updated condition, by creating two counterbalancing lists. In each list, 12 videos were in the incomplete condition and
12 were in the updated condition.
We used a title for each clip and a still image of the first frame of
the clip, blurred with a two-dimensional Gaussian kernel with SD of
25, as a retrieval cue in the recall session. The blurring of the first
frame was done in order to provide participants with a partial cue
and prevent them from simply describing stereotypical actions associated with the spatial location present in the first frame.

To test hypothesis 1, two types of analyses will be run: canonical correlations and a multivariate multiple regression. The first canonical correlation will examine the relationship between the four 2AFC coefficients (AFC.betbat.stepA.coeff, AFC.betbat.stepB.coeff, AFC.deartear.stepA.coeff, AFC.deartear.stepB.coeff) and the two VAS slope measures (VAS.betbat.slope, VAS.deartear.slope). The second canonical correlation will examine the relationship between the four 2AFC coefficients and the two VAS consistency measures (VAS.betbat.consistency, VAS.deartear.consistency). Following up on these correlations, the multivariate multiple regression will have all four 2AFC coefficients as the response, and six variables as the predictors: the two theoretically motivated VAS slope measures, the two theoretically motivated VAS consistency measures, and the two control measures of AXCPT.bin.score and BDS.level in order to account for attention and working memory respectively.  
To test hypothesis 2, a multiple regression model will be fit with Oddity.A.score.exp as the response, and six variables as predictors: AFC.PC1, AFC.PC2, VAS.PC1, VAS.PC2, AXCPT.bin.score, and BDS.level. The 2AFC and VAS predictors are theoretically motivated, while the last two predictors are controlling for attention and working memory.
Details of these analyses (and of the data preprocessing steps and preliminary analyses needed to obtain the variables of interest) are outlined in the attached document.

Canonical correlation 2 revealed that the relationship between

Following up on the correlations, we conducted a multivariate
multiple regression analysis. This enabled us to include all four
2AFC coefficients as the response and all four VAS measures of
interest as predictors, as well as attention and memory measures as
additional control predictors. In doing so, we were able to determine

Using the lm() function, the model equation in R was:
cbind(2AFC bet-bat acoustic cue A slope, 2AFC bet-bat acoustic
cue B slope, 2AFC dear-tear acoustic cue A slope, 2AFC dear-tear
acoustic cue B slope)  VAS bet-bat slope + VAS dear-tear slope
+ VAS bet-bat consistency + VAS dear-tear consistency + AX-CPT
bin score + Digit span level. We then used multivariate tests (Type
II multivariate analysis of variance [MANOVA]) to evaluate the significance of each predictor across the four models, while accounting
for the covariances between coefficients. This was done with the
Anova() function from the car package in R (Fox & Weisberg,
2019).
Output from the multivariate multiple regression model includes
regression tables from four separate regression models, fit with
each 2AFC coefficient as the response; this output is shown in
Tables S4 and S5 in the online supplemental materials for
Experiment 1 and Experiment 2, respectively. Model validation
plots (quantile-quantile plots of residuals, plots of fitted values
against residuals, and plots of Cook’s distance per participant) can
be found in Figures S5–S7 in the online supplemental materials. [...]
In order to test Hypothesis 2, a multiple regression model was fit.
The response was oddity A scores, and the predictors were the first
two principal components derived from the PCA of the 2AFC
coefficients, the first two principal components derived from the
PCA of the VAS measures, and the two control predictors.
Because visualization of the distribution of oddity A scores for both
experiments revealed some negative skew, the scores were exponentially
transformed; models were then fit predicting the scores both with
and without the transformation, and the model with the best performance is reported. Using the lm() function, the model equation in R was: Oddity A score  2AFC principal component 1 + 2AFC principal component 2 + VAS principal component 1 + VAS principal
component 2 + AX-CPT bin score + digit span level. Hypothesis 2
posited that oddity scores would be predicted by the 2AFC and
VAS measures even after accounting for the control predictors.
Results
Hypothesis 2 was not supported; the anticipated predictors did not
significantly predict oddity scores.

Since we had four 2AFC slope measures, two VAS slope
measures and two VAS consistency measures, we tested our hypothesis by first running canonical correlation analyses, which test the
strength of relationships between two sets of variables. 
Canonical correlation 1 revealed that the relationship between
2AFC coefficients and VAS slope measures was small–medium
and statistically insignificant along the first canonical dimension (rc-
= .272, p = .423) and small and statistically insignificant along the
second canonical dimension (rc = .090, p = .855). Canonical correlation 2 revealed that the relationship between
2AFC coefficients and VAS consistency measures was large and significant along the first canonical dimension (rc = .663, p , .001),
and medium–large and significant along the second canonical
dimension (rc = .398, p , .001). 

Following up on the correlations, we conducted a multivariate
multiple regression analysis. This enabled us to include all four
2AFC coefficients as the response and all four VAS measures of
interest as predictors, as well as attention and memory measures as
additional control predictors. 

Hypothesis 2 involved predicting nonnative perception from all
native perception and control measures, which would have resulted
in a model with 10 predictors. To reduce the number of predictors
and thus reduce overfitting while increasing power, dimensionality
of the native perception measures was reduced using PCA, as implemented by the prcomp() function in R.

In order to test Hypothesis 2, a multiple regression model was fit.
The response was oddity A scores, and the predictors were the first
two principal components derived from the PCA of the 2AFC
coefficients, the first two principal components derived from the
PCA of the VAS measures, and the two control predictors.

 We also performed
additional nonpreregistered analyses on the data from both experiments that we had not considered in the preregistration. The
Method section describes the preregistered analyses first, which
consisted of canonical correlation and multivariate multiple regression to assess Hypothesis 1 and of multiple regression to assess
Hypothesis 2. The nonpreregistered analyses, outlined at the end
of the methods, included additional canonical correlations and a
principal component analysis (PCA).

Statistical models

All of our analyses are based on repeated measures within individuals. We will use mixed effects regression to analyze relationships between affective prediction errors and different indicators of aggression. Indicators of aggression can be binary (stole / didn't steal; switched from prior policy / didn't switch) or continuous (amount stolen; difference in amount stolen relative to previous trial; learning rate). The format of the response variable will be reflected in the type of regression model (logistic / linear). Random effects will be included where appropriate to account for variance explained by different subjects, trial numbers, and successful completion of (prior) trials by having pressed the button a sufficient number of times.

The main models of interest predict:

1a) the probability to stick to the chosen policy at t, using affective prediction errors at t-1; we hypothesize a positive relationship
1b) increases in the amount chosen within a given policy from t-1 to t, using affective prediction errors at t-1; we hypothesize a positive relationship

2) affective prediction errors at t using policy choice (steal/earn) as a predictor; we expect steal trials to be associated with more positive prediction errors

As manipulation check, we will also test whether aggression increases as identification with the target decreases.

Analyses that don't rely on repeated measures (e.g., group identification by political party, where participants are expected to identify more with their in-group) will be conducted using standard linear regression.
[...]
Inference criteria

We will rely on 95% confidence intervals and the p < .05 criterion to infer statistical significance, including one-sided tests according to predictions, as well as Bayes Factors > 10, where appropriate.

All analyses were conducted using linear regression models
accounting for the distribution of the response variable and
repeated measures. Speci cally, we used logistic regression for
dichotomous outcomes—such as aggressive versus nonaggressive
policies, or policy switching versus policy persistence, from t− 1
to t—implemented with the“glmer” function in the“lme4” pack-
age (Bates et al., 2015). Continuous outcomes—such as increases
in the amount chosen from t− 1 to t—were analyzed using linear
regression using the“lmer” function from the same package.
Both approaches included random effects (intercept and slope
depending on the model t; see below) to cluster error related to
repeated measures, such as participant ID, trial number, and policy
type as applicable. For each analysis, we selected the model with
the lowest Akaike information criterion out of a range of models
up to the maximal random effects structure that still allowed
model convergence; in the case of equal Akaike information crite-
rion values, the model closer to the maximal speci cation was
selected. We assessed normality in tted residuals using the
DHARMa package (Hartig, 2018). This was particularly important
to ensure that deviations from normality in the underlying data
(e.g., multimodality) did not violate the assumptions of the regres-
sion models we used. Partial eta squared effect sizes (η2) were
calculated by taking the estimated xed effects and dividing
them by the square root of the sum of random effect variances
of the corresponding model (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018).
