Statistical analysis will be conducted using mixed-effects models fit using the lme4 package in R. 

For the reading time data in the eye-tracking task, reading times will be log-transformed to remove any skew in the data (see Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016). Linear mixed effects models will be fit to each of the three reading time measures, containing fixed main effects and interactions for group (L1/L2), sentence region (critical/spillover), sentence plausibility (plausible/implausible) and distractor plausibility (plausible/implausible). Each fixed effect will be sum-coded (-1/1). Random effects for subjects and items will be included using the “maximal” random-effects structure that converges (Barr, 2013; Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily, 2013). For reading times, random effects of trial will also be included (see Cunnings & Sturt, 2018). Example code is as below:

model = lmer(log(rt) ~ group * region * plausibility * distractor + (1+region*plausibility*distractor|subject) + (1+group*region*plausibility*distractor|item) + (1+region|trial), data = rt_data)

In the case of interactions between plausibility and distractor, nested contrasts will be conducted at the two levels of plausibility to examine interference effects. In the case of any interactions with region and/or group, separate analyses will be conducted on each region and/or group as appropriate.

For the accuracy data in the second (non eye-tracking) reading task, analysis will be conducted using generalised (binomial) mixed models. Sum-coded fixed effects will include group (L1/L2), sentence type (filled gap/no filled gap) and distractor plausibility (plausible/implausible). Models will be fit with the maximal random effects structure that converges. See example code below:

model = glmer(acc ~ group * type * plausibility + (1+type*plausibility|subject) + (1+group*type*plausibility|item), family=binomial, data = acc_data)

In the case of interactions between sentence type and plausibility, nested contrasts will be conducted at the two levels of sentence type to examine interference effects. In the case of any interactions with group, separate analyses will be conducted on each group as appropriate.

If the maximal model in any analysis fails to converge, the model will be refit removing the random correlation parameters. If this model still fails to converge, the random effects parameter that accounts for the least variance in the data will be iteratively removed until convergence is achieved.
paper_c1: When fitting the models, we log-transformed reading times to reduce the skew of residuals. Following Cunnings and Sturt (2018), we analyzed the critical and spillover regions in the same model. Thus, each model contained fixed effects of sum-coded group (L1/L2), region (critical region/ spillover region), filler (plausible/implausible), distractor (plausible/implausible), and their interactions. The models also included random intercepts for participants, items and trials, random slopes for each within-participants, within-items, and within-trials fixed effect and random correlations between random intercepts and slopes (Barr et al., 2013). When this maximal model failed to converge, we initially removed the random correlations. If the model still did not converge, we iteratively removed the random effect accounting for the least variance until the model converged (Barr et al., 2013). We estimated p values from the t distribution (Baayen, 2008) and interpreted p values smaller than .05 as significant. When a significant interaction appeared, follow-up analyses examined nested simple effects of theoretical interest within a single model (Schad et al., 2021).

1. We hypothesize that participants will learn the PC signal carried by the target and demonstrate a significant ISPC effect with the training items.

2. We hypothesize that the ISPC effect will mainly be driven by the incongruent trials compared to the congruent trials for the training items.

3. If the retrieval and execution of item-specific control settings are automatic, for the participants showing an ISPC effect with the training items, they will demonstrate a significant ISPC effect with the transfer items because the same relevant dimension (color) is presented. If the retrieval and execution of item-specific control settings are not automatic (i.e., there is either context- or task-dependency), even for the participants showing an ISPC effect with the training items, they will not demonstrate a significant ISPC effect with the transfer items.

4. In addition to testing the third hypothesis by examining the ISPC effect, we will also test this hypothesis by examining the difference between incongruent items presented with target colors that were MC and MI previously. Apparatus and Stimuli
This and the other three experiments reported subsequently were
conducted online using the JavaScript library jsPsych (De Leeuw,
2015). All visual stimuli were presented on a gray background. In
each trial, a letter was presented in black font surrounded by a colored outline square. A centrally positioned white plus sign served as
fixation point. For each participant, two letters were randomly
selected out of a letter set (i.e., all consonants except L, Q, P, R, Q)
with one each assigned to the left index and left middle finger
response. Similarly, two colors were randomly selected out of a
color set (i.e., red, green, blue) with one each assigned to the right
index and right middle finger response, respectively. For half of the
participants, the letter task was the first task and the color task the
second task whereas this mapping was reversed for the other half of
participants. Responses were key presses on the “Q,”“W,”“O,” and
“P” keys of a standard QWERTZ computer keyboard.

Registration prior to accessing the data: As of the date of submission, the data exist, but has not been analyzed to answer the research questions outlined above.

The current pre-registration focuses on a subset of relevant variables collected in a main study (see variable section for details). We pre-registered the data collection procedure for the main study at https://osf.io/j2a9g/. Analyses will be performed using data from all participants who pass exclusion criteria in the data cleaning phase, as outlined in Section 27 below.

Data will be made available on OSF as part of the publication process. The study codebook outlining survey items is included in the data collection pre-registration (https://osf.io/j2a9g).

Data collection procedures
11.1.	Study duration (number of days):
Data collection lasted for 15 consecutive days in total. On Day 0, participants completed the baseline survey. On Day 1 to 14, participants completed one daily survey per day.

11.2.	Type of sampling scheme:
After completing the baseline survey, eligible participants received one daily survey between 5:30 PM and 6:30 PM for the next 14 consecutive days. Each daily survey expired at midnight.

11.3.	Total number and type of items (open-ended or closed) and estimated questionnaire duration:
The baseline survey included a combination of validated and purpose-designed scales to assess time-invariant individual difference variables. Following a pilot, we estimated the completion time for the baseline survey to be approximately 30 minutes, although participants appeared to complete the baseline more quickly than this estimate. The daily survey consisted of 62 questions (12 of which were relevant to the current study). Following a pilot, we estimated the completion time for each daily survey to range between 5 to 6 minutes.

11.4.	Time-out specifications:
Each daily survey was sent out between 5:30 PM and 6:30 PM and expired at midnight.

11.5.	Additional passive monitoring:
Not applicable

11.6.	Incentivization and increasing participant engagement:
Participants were compensated monetarily for their involvement via an incentive scheme, contingent on their compliance. The incentive scheme was structured as follows:
•	Baseline survey completed = £3.50
•	1 daily survey completed = £0.70
(Total £9.80 if all 14 surveys are completed)
•	Bonus if at least 13 surveys are completed = £2.00
All participants were informed of the incentive structure prior to completing the study and could keep track of their compliance on Prolific. Participants received a reminder via Prolific on the seventh day of daily survey, to increase their engagement and compliance, if they had completed fewer than 6 out of 7 daily surveys.

11.7.	Please indicate any additional details that are relevant to the daily diary data collection procedure:
Screener session: A description of the project was advertised via Prolific. Participants who had chosen to take part completed a brief 4-5-minute screener survey. Participants were compensated for completing the screener (£0.50). This screener survey was used to determine eligibility for this study, which included participants who:
A.	Had at least one current secret, and
B.	Did not report having a diagnosis of a mental health disorder

Baseline session: In the baseline session, participants read a plain language statement introducing the study and provided informed consent. Next, they completed time-invariant individual difference measures in the baseline survey.

Daily survey period: The 14-day daily survey period began the day after the baseline session. Participants had the option to contact the researchers via Prolific with questions during this period.

We will run mixed effects models. The outcome variable will be each emotion regulation strategy. We will include one person-level predictor variable in each model – each feature of the secret. These predictors will be grand-mean centered. We will include a random intercept for participant.

If the strategic curiosity condition leads to more uncertaintydirected exploration and sensitivity to environmental features—
relative to the control condition—we anticipated children in this
condition would search more flexibly and strategically (e.g., search
more persistently in a tank after observing evidence of high-reward
density) than children in the control condition and ultimately find
more creatures. Additionally, although our search task differed in
several ways from foraging and bandit tasks traditionally used to study
explore/exploit decisions (e.g., Hutchinson et al., 2008), it posed a
similar dilemma—children faced a trade-off between searching the
current tank in depth (exploiting their current location) and exploring
the possibility of finding more sea creatures in another tank. The two
storybooks, too, had related themes—the strategic curiosity story
emphasized exploring to gain new information, while the control
story emphasized exploiting information that was already known.
This might translate into distinct search patterns, with children in the
control condition searching more deeply within tanks and children in
the strategic curiosity condition searching more broadly across tanks

Sample size
Our target sample size in the United States is 132 subjects. We will attempt to recruit 147 subjects assuming a low level of attrition in the full study sample (10%). 

Sample size rationale
Previous research has detected a medium effect of linguistic priming in a story context on curiosity (Dubey et al., 2019). Because this effect size is based on an adult sample, we took a conservative approach in our power analysis to correct for bias due to uncertainty (Anderson et al., 2017). A power analysis correcting for uncertainty using the BUCCS package in R revealed that 132 subjects with 80% power and an alpha level of .05 would be sufficient to detect an effect of medium size.

Stopping rule
We do not plan to stop data collection until we reach our target sample size.

In the Agency task, we hypothesise that the level of tactile manipulations will be inversely related to agency ratings, similar to temporal and spatial manipulations. 

In the MetAgency task, we hypothesise that metacognitive efficiency (measured as M-ratio) will be different between conditions that differ in the experimental manipulation (described below), once we account for first-order discrimination performance. 
In particular, if tactile information contributes especially to the subjective experience of agency, we expect to find higher metacognitive sensitivity in an agency discrimination task that involves violations of tactile predictions, as compared to other (spatial or temporal) prediction violations. 
If, on the other hand, tactile predictions do not play a special role on the subjective experience of agency, and predictions on any sensory modality are equally important, we will see no differences in metacognitive sensitivity.
